name: Mississippi Today
title: Senate Corrections Chairman Juan Barnett resigns from Legislature
description: Sen. Juan Barnett is seen on the Senate floor at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Feb. 12, 2026.
text:
Sen. Juan Barnett, a three-term Democratic legislator from Heidelberg and chairman of the Senate Corrections Committee, resigned from the Legislature on Monday, Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann said in a statement. 
It’s unclear why Barnett resigned, and he did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but he has dealt with health issues that caused him to miss several weeks of this year’s regular legislative session.
“We thank Senator Barnett for his years of service to the state of Mississippi and wish him a happy and well-deserved retirement,” Hosemann said in a statement. 
Barnett took office in 2016 and has served as the chairman of the Senate Corrections Committee since 2020.  He has represented portions of Forrest, Jasper and Jones counties in the Senate. 
Barnett in the past pushed for earlier release and shortened sentences for many incarcerated in Mississippi prisons, despite his father being shot to death in the early 1990s while Barnett was in the Army deployed to Iraq, and the shooter receiving a relatively short sentence. Barnett said he believes in forgiveness and giving people second chances.
Barnett missed several weeks of the 2026 legislative session because of an extended illness. Gov. Tate Reeves will now have 30 days to set the date for a special election.
While he was absent from the Capitol, legislation that attempted to improve medical care in Mississippi prisons died on key deadlines. The vice chairman of the committee at the time said she let the legislation die at Barnett’s direction. 
Before serving in the Legislature, Barnett was the mayor of his hometown of Heidelberg. 
Mississippi Today reporter Michael Goldberg contributed to this report.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: ‘Not the place to commit financial crimes’: Utah aims to better fight complex scams
description: Utah is stepping up its efforts to investigate scams and connect the dots between them with a new hub that’s the second of its kind in the nation.
text:
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown speaks at a news conference announcing the state's new Financial Crimes Intelligence Center on Aug. 31, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)Utah is stepping up its efforts to investigate scams and connect the dots between them with a new hub that’s the second of its kind in the nation, state leaders said Monday.
They want the Financial Crimes Intelligence Center in the Utah attorney general’s office to form a new line of defense against increasingly sophisticated operations, including those using artificial intelligence to multiply their reach, said Utah Attorney General Derek Brown.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The problem is growing, he told reporters, with Utahns losing $108 million to financial crimes last year and almost $60 million so far this year. Once someone’s been scammed, Brown noted a bank typically flags the problem, a police department will open a case and a hotline will field a call from the victim seeking help. 
“But ultimately, none of these organizations are talking with each other,” Brown said. “So it’s hard to know if they’re part of a larger, organized crime ring. There’s a gap. And today the FCIC is filling that gap.” 
Utah lawmakers this year gave their support to the center, committing to $1.7 million in yearly funding. Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore, who sponsored the budget request, said it fits with the Legislature’s recent move to protect digital identity and sends a strong message. 
Lawmakers convene in the House Chamber at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the first day of the legislative session, Tuesday, Jan. 20, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“I think this will signal that we are not the place to commit financial crimes,” Cullimore, R-Sandy, said during Monday’s news conference at the state Capitol. 
As they pieced together the plan for the center, state officials met with law enforcers in Texas to learn about a state fraud intelligence center there, Brown said after the news conference. The Utah team’s goal is to bring in enough information to recognize patterns, he told Utah News Dispatch. 
“And frankly, AI is going to help us do that as well,” Brown said, adding that component is still taking shape. “You know, we can use the same tools that they use — to benefit us.”
He’ll measure the success of the program in part by how much money is returned to victims after judges order restitution, Brown said. But it will be more difficult to know how many people never fall victim because of prevention and heightened awareness, he added.  
To fight elder fraud, a top Utah law enforcer is meeting with seniors around the state 

The center’s employees include two prosecutors, two investigators, a forensic accountant, an analyst and a paralegal. They report to a division director in the attorney general’s office overseeing mortgage and financial fraud cases, Brown said. 
Surrounded by representatives from banking and credit union associations at the news conference, Brown and Cullimore said Utahns who fall victim to fraud should not feel ashamed. 
Cullimore said within the last week, someone in his household accidentally gave credit card information to a fake website. And Brown recounted how an attorney friend lost millions to a sophisticated real estate scam.
 “I just want you to reach out, I want you to report it, because a $30,000 fraud that takes place in Cache County and a $30,000 fraud taking place in Washington County may actually be connected,” Brown said. “Our job is to identify that connection.”
Howard Headlee, president of the Utah Bankers Association, added it’s important to file a report right away so investigators can get to work. 
“In these cases, time is of the essence. Time is critical,” Headlee said.  
To report fraud to the center, visit its website at fraud.agutah.gov.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bottoms ups the ante in feud over debates in race for Georgia governor
description: Months after the campaigns of Republican Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms first issued challenges to the other over when, where and how to debate ahead of the November elections, there’s still little agreement on how voters will hear from each of the two candidates for governor. So far, both campaigns have agreed to […]
text:
Democratic Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson, both candidates for governor, speak at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, on Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderMonths after the campaigns of Republican Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms first issued challenges to the other over when, where and how to debate ahead of the November elections, there’s still little agreement on how voters will hear from each of the two candidates for governor.
So far, both campaigns have agreed to only one town hall-style debate hosted by Atlanta News First and Gray Media on Oct. 6. 
The Bottoms campaign first challenged Jackson to three debates in June, to which the Jackson campaign responded by proposing one debate. Nearly two months later, Bottoms agreed Monday to it and is now pushing for five more.
“Georgians deserve to hear directly from candidates for public office with multiple debates around the state,” Bottoms said in a statement. “I’m ready to debate Rick Jackson in Atlanta, Macon and Savannah.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Aside from the ANF debate both candidates agreed to, Bottoms is also challenging Jackson to the Atlanta Press Club Loudermilk-Young debate on Oct. 12, another on Sept. 17 hosted by Middle Georgia Matters, an 11Alive debate on Sept. 22, a WJCL-TV debate on Oct. 13 and one hosted by CNN at an undetermined date.
The Jackson campaign criticized the move, with campaign spokesman Garrison Douglas saying that “only the flailing campaign of a failed politician would spend more than six weeks ducking a debate, then suddenly demand six of them after Georgians begin to learn the truth about her disastrous record as mayor of Atlanta.”
The Democratic Party of Georgia instead focused on Jackson not yet accepting the Atlanta Press Club debate. Jackson participated in the press club debate during the Republican primary but cited a scheduling conflict with the debate scheduled for the primary runoff with Lt. Gov. Burt Jones.
“Over two months later and Jackson still won’t commit to a debate that gubernatorial candidates in both parties have participated in for more than twenty years,” said DPG spokesperson Jake Strickland.
The Jackson campaign has not yet indicated a reason for not accepting the Atlanta Press Club debate, where a panel of journalists ask the candidates questions.
Debates are unlikely to change voters’ minds, but participating in them provides candidates a massive platform to build name recognition and excitement amongst voters, said University of Georgia political communications professor David Clementson. 
Clementson said  it’s in both candidates’ interest to participate in as many debates as possible in what he called the “the single most watched political events by far.”
“The upside far outweighs the downsides for both of them, as far as any kind of risk versus reward,” Clementson said. “The rewards outweigh the risk for both of them to be in as many debates as possible to get attention to help boost their profile amongst their bases. They need to remind their supporters, their partisan-aligned supporters, who they are and that they’re running for governor and why they need to get out and vote in this election.”
Candidates can miss on the opportunity to mobilize their supporters by skipping or limiting debates, but Jackson, who won the Republican nomination for governor despite skipping the Atlanta Press Club debate during the runoff, could be feeling confident that he can succeed again in November without it, Clementson said.
“That might be his thinking there, but he needs to be reminding the general election Republican voter base,” he said, adding that “the effect of general election debates is crystallizing the support, crystallizing your base, solidifying your support base, because each side is going to need their respective base to turn out and vote for them in this election.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico officials say 89,000 residents may lose coverage under Medicaid work requirements
description: Upcoming work requirements contained in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” could mean that roughly one-tenth of all New Mexico Medicaid recipients lose their coverage, leaders of state agencies said in a virtual news conference Monday.
text:
New Mexico Health Care Authority officials said at a news conference Aug. 31, 2026, that upcoming work requirements in the federal “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” may result in 89,000 New Mexicans losing Medicaid coverage. (Getty Images)Upcoming work requirements contained in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” could mean that roughly one-tenth of all New Mexico Medicaid recipients lose their coverage, leaders of state agencies said in a virtual news conference Monday.
Beginning in January, the new law requires that some Medicaid recipients aged 19 to 64 work, volunteer or attend school or job training 80 hours a week to continue receiving coverage.  SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
To raise awareness about the change, more than 230,000 New Mexicans will soon receive turquoise envelopes in the mail that lay out the new requirements, as well as connect Medicaid recipients to state resources designed to help them stay covered, state leaders said. 
Still, Health Care Authority officials predict that roughly 89,000 Medicaid recipients will lose coverage due to those requirements.
Department of Workforce Solutions Secretary Sarita Nair said the state offers an array of services to job seekers. She pointed to the 24 America’s Jobs centers across the state, as well as the New Mexico Jobs website, as resources available to those who risk losing coverage. 
“You don’t have to navigate that process alone. You don’t have to know exactly what career you’re looking for before you walk through our doors,” Nair said. “That’s what we’re here for — to help you figure that out and to provide you with the tools to succeed.”
More than 825,000 New Mexicans receive Medicaid in New Mexico, according to the Health Care Authority. 
Even if they met the work requirements, roughly 2,300 immigrants may lose eligibility due to changes in the law impacting some categories of immigrants. Moreover, the number of residents losing coverage could grow to more than 100,000 due to a new requirement that recipients affirm eligibility every six months versus annually.
Calculating the total number of Medicaid recipients projected to lose coverage is difficult, officials said, because the recipients may lose eligibility for two or more of the above reasons. 
Still, Health Care Authority Kari Armijo said that the agency is doing all it can to prevent those coverage reductions and urged recipients to open the turquoise envelopes and reach out to her office. She stressed that simply receiving the letter does not mean that a recipient lost coverage. 
“We do recognize, after having gone through all of those complicated changes, that these federal changes are really complex,” she said. “We’re not expecting our customers to figure this out on their own.”

name: VTDigger
title: ‘Stronger now than it was’: Quechee Gorge Bridge reopens with new suicide barriers
description:
The upgrades to the bridge overlooking Vermont’s deepest natural canyon are meant to save lives.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Stronger now than it was’: Quechee Gorge Bridge reopens with new suicide barriers.
text:
From left, Nancy Cullen, of Houston, Texas, Gloria Curtis, of Edmond, Okla., Jeff Curtis, of Fort Worth, Texas, and Joyce Brimer, of Edmond, Okla., take a selfie on the recently renovated Quechee Gorge Bridge in Quechee, Vt., on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. The group has been visiting Meredith, N.H., and they chose to visit the gorge because they said they wanted to step a foot in Vermont. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

This story by Sofia Langlois was first published in the Valley News on Aug. 28, 2026.HARTFORD — Inside the gift shop next to the Quechee Gorge Bridge, Pam Kendall was pleased to see the new and improved structure finally completed, though she doesn’t agree with every aspect of the bridge’s revamped design.
“I feel the rails are way too low,” she said of the barriers between the sidewalk and road. Kendall worries those guardrails are wide enough for children to climb and sit on, and if a parent isn’t paying attention, they could fall right into traffic.
Other changes to the bridge over the Ottauquechee River include metal barriers to help prevent death by suicide — a tragedy the popular tourist destination knows all too well.
“If you grew up here and you’re old enough, most people know someone, unfortunately,” said Lt. Will Furnari of the Hartford Police Department. “Every time I drive through, I scan the fence just as a force of habit.”
The upgrades to the bridge overlooking Vermont’s deepest natural canyon are meant to save lives. While suicide calls have increased in Hartford, a police department study found that incidents at the gorge declined since the state put up a temporary chain-link fence in 2018.
Before that fence went up, incidents involving the gorge accounted for about 37% of suicide calls in Hartford. Since it went up, that figure dropped to 10%, according to a report by the department’s data and crime analyst, Amie Wunderlich.
Visitors at Quechee Gorge will now find green steel rails that are over 9 feet tall and curved at the top, separated by about 6 inches. With the project complete, locals and tourists alike are experiencing a different version of the landmark for the first time.

Pedestrians walk along the Quechee Gorge Bridge in Quechee, Vt., on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Construction on the bridge, which began in summer 2023, included rehabilitation of the bridge deck, installation of new safety barriers and reinforcement of the steel arch. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

A three-year project
Every day, about 9,500 cars drive across the Quechee Gorge Bridge. The last upgrade was back in the 1980s, though it undergoes regular maintenance, according to Vermont Department of Transportation project manager JB McCarthy.
The recent work addressed significant deterioration of the structural steel beneath the deck, cleaned and repainted the bridge, expanded its sidewalk and added pedestrian fencing.
The crew widened sidewalks from about 3.5 feet to 6 feet to afford more space. One of the major safety issues was when people would step back to take a picture of the gorge and stand in the travel lane, said McCarthy.
Workers extended the sidewalks west toward Woodstock and east to the visitor center. McCarthy noted that in the past, tourists were parking on the shoulder and getting out into the travel lane to look at the view.
“It really wasn’t a safe situation,” he said.
The renovations have been in discussion for about a decade. The state installed a chain-link fence and held meetings with the town of Hartford and the Hartford Area Chamber of Commerce to come up with a permanent safety solution.

Manager Pam Kendall organizes merchandise at Quechee Gorge Gifts in Quechee, Vt., on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Since construction on the Quechee Gorge Bridge ended “we’ve been so much busier,” Kendall said. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

The bidding took some time due to the length of the project, but the state awarded it to Harrison and Burrowes, a bridge contractor based in Glenmont, New York, for $22 million.
Although the anticipated length of time was two and a half to three years, the crew discovered more steel deterioration than expected, which prolonged the length of the project by six months.
McCarthy said that before the work began, using the bridge wasn’t a safety risk because it’s inspected every two years. However, the new design is safer for both motorists and pedestrians.
“The bridge is actually stronger now than it was,” said McCarthy, who added that the structure has done well for a bridge designed and built in 1911.
Only one travel lane was open to cross the bridge throughout the construction period, including during winter. The contractor used an automated light system with a camera to monitor queues and change the signals.
“We really didn’t get any complaints from people because of the lights,” said McCarthy, who added that one-lane traffic was the only option, “short of building another separate temporary bridge.”
The cost ended up being about 15% to 20% higher than expected. It was covered 80% by federal funds and 20% by state funds. McCarthy said the cleaning and repainting made up about half the cost of the project.
One major goal was to lengthen the barrier at the overlook. The railings are currently about 9.5 feet, curved at the top, and difficult to climb over, which was one of the design criteria.
For many years, there was a 3.5-foot railing there.

Pedestrians keep an eye out for traffic as they cross the road near the Quechee Gorge Bridge in Quechee, Vt., on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Pam Kendall, manager of Quechee Gorge Gifts, said she is concerned about the limited safety mechanisms included in the bridge project, including crosswalks with no flashing lights and a low barrier between traffic and sidewalks that is easy for children to climb on. “Cars don’t stop,” Kendall said. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

What do people think?
Massachusetts resident Kathy Garland has visited the Quechee Gorge bridge three times: before construction, during construction and on Tuesday, with it fully reopened.
“Now it looks absolutely beautiful,” she said. “It’s really pretty.”
As for the new railing, Garland feels it doesn’t obstruct the view and the green paint is a “nice touch.” She and her husband, Dave, said the construction seemed worth the effort, especially with the wider sidewalk.
Between the sidewalk and the road are smaller green rails, about 1 foot high.
“That is not good,” Mugzy Undemir said, pointing to the railing after her 6-year-old son started to climb on one of them. Undemir, a first-time visitor, would like to see those lifted up to hip height to be safer.
North Carolina resident Griffin Tracy didn’t plan to stop off in Quechee, but pulled over when he saw the view.
“I can tell it’s new,” Tracy said of the bridge.
Walking across, Tracy said motorists seem to be observant of the crosswalk and that the 35 mph speed limit helps keep it safe for pedestrians.

Mike Reardon, of Lebanon, N.H., leans in as his dog Bowser, 11, sniffs his cheek while sitting on a rock in the Ottauquechee in Quechee, Vt., on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. The trail under the bridge has reopened, allowing pedestrians to hike down to the gorge from the parking lot on the north side of Route 4 in addition to the trailhead near the Quechee Gorge Visitor Center. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

At Quechee Gorge Gifts & Sportswear, Kendall the manager is glad to see the project finally completed, with more customers coming in, though she thinks the final result could be a bit safer.
Over the past few years, the one-lane traffic made it hard for people to pull in and out of the parking lot right next to the bridge, where the store and a snack bar operate. Kendall believes they lost business from buses parking farther down the road at the visitor center, plus foot traffic when half the sidewalk was closed.
The degree of road traffic depended on the day, but sometimes it took up to 10 minutes to pass through. Kendall recalled being stuck all the way back by Quechee Gorge Village, which is half a mile down the road.
“The lights were terrible. Half the cars would run the light just to get through,” said Kendall.
As for the rails preventing people from going over the bridge, Kendall has no problem with those. In her opinion, the construction time was worth upgrading the bridge she started working near eight years ago.

Maps and tourism brochures sit in a kiosk near the Quechee Gorge in Quechee, Vt., on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. The steel arch structure that supports the Quechee Gorge Bridge today was originally build in 1911 as a railroad bridge. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

Prevention efforts
Furnari, who serves as the community outreach lieutenant with the Hartford police, has no idea how many people traveled to the bridge and decided not to end their lives. But there is data from every time police showed up to help someone.
Between May 2014 and April 2026, police recorded 79 suicide incidents related to the gorge, with seven resulting in death. The others were attempts or ideations that were communicated to others.
“For as long as I’ve been alive, it’s a place where people have gone and killed themselves,” said Furnari, who added that the best thing to do is make the act more challenging.
Of the total incidents, 48 occurred during the four-year period before the chain-link fence went up, and 29 occurred with the barrier installed. The pre-fence average was about 10.9 per year, and the post-fence average dropped to 4.1 per year.
There is currently a crisis hotline sign by the crosswalk. Since 2018, call boxes that automatically dialed 911 were placed near the bridge with phones, but were removed a couple of months ago.
“They were never intended to last long term,” Furnari said of the phones.
As for the green arched railings, Furnari considers them a balance from an aesthetic perspective and a safety perspective. The curved fence, if nothing else, he said, adds time for police to arrive or for someone to intervene.
“I’m of the opinion that we should do everything we can to save as many lives as we can,” said Furnari.
The most recent suicide occurred during construction. Back in April, a woman got onto the bridge through an open corner and ended her life.
“They’ve addressed that weakness,” said Furnari.
The suicidal ideation at the tourist destination represents a wider trend that’s not unique to the Quechee Gorge. For example, the Piscataqua Bridge on Interstate 95 between Portsmouth, New Hampshire, and Kittery, Maine, saw three suicides in a 24-hour period back in May. Although the bridge has suicide hotline signs, some have pushed for a physical barrier.
Also this spring, a Massachusetts woman allegedly killed her two children, then came to the Quechee Gorge Bridge to take her own life. A family member reported that she “tried to jump off, but couldn’t,” according to WCAX.
Furnari said the gorge’s popularity as a tourist destination means more people are present to intervene or report it.
“We can’t change the geography, so the best thing we can do is make it harder for people to utilize,” said Furnari.
Those struggling or in crisis are encouraged to text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and speak with a trained counselor. Hartford police have a mental health liaison who can be reached at 802-295-9425.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Transgender student drops lawsuit challenging SC’s school bathroom law
description: The student moved out of the state after experiencing harassment for being transgender, his attorneys saidThe student moved out of the state after experiencing harassment for being transgender, his attorneys said.
text:
A student dropped a lawsuit challenging a budget clause that required transgender students use the bathroom aligned with their sex at birth. (File photo/Getty Images)COLUMBIA — A lawsuit over which bathrooms transgender students can use came to an end after the student suing moved to a different state, attorneys on the case said.
The transgender high school sophomore, who is unnamed in court documents, filed the lawsuit in federal court in November 2024, when the Berkeley County student was in eighth grade. It challenged a budget clause that barred K-12 public schools from letting transgender students use multi-stalled bathrooms that don’t align with their sex at birth.
Schools that gave permission risked losing a quarter of their state funding.
Transgender SC student drops appeal in bathroom lawsuit after switching to virtual school

The student withdrew from in-person classes last year, with attorneys also citing bullying he faced for being transgender. Berkeley County school officials disputed that description and said the district “is committed to preventing and correcting discrimination and harassment of any form.”
Outside of school, the student “continued to face transphobic harassment,” according to a recent statement from Public Justice, which represented the student in the case. He and his family moved to another state, which attorneys didn’t name, so the student “can attend school in a safe, inclusive learning environment,” the statement reads.
“Like all children, John has a right to attend school in a safe environment where he is respected and valued,” the statement read. “South Carolina, however, has actively worked to foment a hostile environment within its schools and the state as a whole.”
The budget clause, which is technically a one-year law, was superseded earlier this year by a permanent law that extended the rules to state-funded universities.
Public Justice still believes the law is unconstitutional, according to the statement.
Attorneys have repeatedly pointed to a case in Virginia where the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals — the same circuit that would hear South Carolina’s case — ruled in 2021 that a transgender student could use the bathroom and locker room of his choice, overturning a state law. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the case, allowing that decision to stand.
Attorneys for the state disagreed, saying in court documents the law fell in line with a growing consensus among judges about what fell under the constitutional right to privacy. Schools could make different arrangements for transgender students to use the bathroom, preventing discrimination, attorneys argued in court filings.
The case has spent much of the past two years on hold as the nation’s high court considered a different case about whether Idaho and West Virginia could bar transgender athletes from playing on the sports team of their choice.
On June 30, justices ruled 6-3 those laws could stand, which also upheld South Carolina’s similar “Save Women Sports Act,” signed in 2022.
U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel, who was presiding over the case involving the Berkeley County student, told both sides to argue why that ruling on sports did or didn’t apply to the bathroom law.
SC Senate approves bill restricting transgender bathroom use at K-12 schools and colleges

But last month, before that deadline, the student dropped the case.
The attorney general’s office didn’t respond Monday to a request for comment about the case’s end. Attorney General Alan Wilson previously called the dismissal of an appeal in the case “a major win for common sense and for South Carolina families.”
In September 2025, part of the case reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled Berkeley County School District had to let the student use the bathroom of his choice as the lawsuit continued. The decision applied only to the student suing and didn’t reflect the court’s opinions on the case itself, only the question of whether the law should apply as the case played out, justices wrote at the time.
This is the second time a challenge to South Carolina’s laws about transgender rights have been dismissed without a ruling.
The American Civil Liberties Union, along with a group of transgender adults and children, dropped a lawsuit last year challenging a state law that barred all gender transition treatments for youth and prohibited taxpayer dollars from going toward procedures for adults.
That decision came after the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a similar law in Tennessee banning gender transition treatments for transgender youth. That decision also sent two cases about whether health insurance coverage should include the treatments for transgender adults to the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals for consideration.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee approves license for nuclear fusion facility in Clinton, Bull Run Energy Complex
description: Officials approved an application for the state’s first nuclear fusion site, as Tennessee leaders continue to advance their multi-year plan to make the state an epicenter of a new type of energy technology. The Tennessee Department of Environmental Conservation approved Type One Energy’s permit to break ground on a research and development facility for nucle[...]
text:
The Tennessee Valley Authority's Sequoyah Nuclear Plant in Chattanooga, one of three nuclear facilities the energy giant operates. Tennessee is under consideration for a U.S. Department of Energy program to increase the state's nuclear capacity. (Photo: Facebook)Officials approved an application for the state’s first nuclear fusion site, as Tennessee leaders continue to advance their multi-year plan to make the state an epicenter of a new type of energy technology.
The Tennessee Department of Environmental Conservation approved Type One Energy’s permit to break ground on a research and development facility for nuclear fusion power at the Bull Run Energy Complex run by the Tennessee Valley Authority, TVA.
The Bull Run complex is located in Anderson County across the river from Oak Ridge, a city made famous for its integral part in the Manhattan Project to build an atomic bomb during World War II.
Type One Energy will break ground on the campus this year, with plans to finish it by 2034, the company said in a news release announcing the permit approval. The campus will allow the company to work on research in tandem with the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, TVA, and the University of Tennessee.
The company hopes to build a 400-megawatt nuclear fusion power plant in a second phase of the project.
Tennessee, local governments will forgo sales taxes on $4.5B nuclear facility

For several years, Tennessee has been clearing the way for nuclear energy-related projects, after federal regulators agreed in 2023 to treat fusion facilities under a less stringent regulatory framework than full-scale nuclear fission reactors.
Nuclear fission reactors, the traditional way nuclear energy is produced, carry a risk of meltdown and produce radioactive waste.
Nuclear fusion facilities carry almost no risk of a meltdown and no high-level radioactive waste, according to the International Atomic Energy Commission, but the technology is relatively new and still needs to be proven as a reliable energy source.
Tennessee wrote new rules classifying nuclear projects as green energy, allowing them to qualify for several tax breaks and offering multimillion-dollar state grants to companies like Type One.
The state is also a finalist for the nuclear lifecycle campus, a federal program designed to provide financial incentives to states to bring in nuclear power plants and agree to store the radioactive waste.
Gov. Bill Lee called the lifecycle campus an “incredible opportunity” and touted the Type One Energy project as the “next generation” in creating “abundant American energy.”
But several state representatives have opposed Tennessee taking on more nuclear projects.
State Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, and state Rep. Ed Butler, a Rickman Republican, questioned in separate letters the economic value of any new nuclear project if the state has to agree to store radioactive waste.

name: WyoFile
title: Family sues Campbell County, sheriff’s employees over inmate’s death
description:
Kenneth Durrah died naked and strapped to a restraint chair. His family alleges deputies used excessive force and ignored his medical needs. 
The post Family sues Campbell County, sheriff’s employees over inmate’s death appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A civil rights lawsuit filed Monday alleges law enforcement used excessive force and showed deliberate indifference to the medical needs of Kenneth Durrah, a prisoner who died naked and strapped to a restraint chair in the Campbell County jail in 2022. 
Durrah’s family, represented by Denver attorney Darold Killmer, filed the lawsuit Monday against Campbell County, Sheriff Scott Matheny and several other individuals in the county sheriff’s office. 
“They murdered my brother,” Joshua Durrah, the man’s brother, said in a Monday statement. “He needed help and medical treatment. Instead, they crushed the life out of him, stripped him naked, and strapped him in a chair to die. He could not breathe, and he told them so, begging for his life. They ignored his cries for help.” 
Photos of Kenneth Durrah included in the lawsuit filed by his family, preceded by the text, “Kenneth Durrah was a beloved brother and father, and his family continues togrieve his loss and always will.” (Court record)
In the hours preceding Durrah’s death, he had reported chest pain and trouble breathing. Medics cleared him to remain in jail. Shortly after, detention deputies saw him swallow what appeared to be methamphetamine. They restrained Durrah facedown on the floor and then put him in a restraint chair in a booking area cell where they checked on him periodically. 
Video from the jail captured Durrah telling the guards that the restraint chair straps were too tight. “I can’t breathe,” he called out. “I’m dying. Help!” But the deputies told him he was breathing fine and didn’t adjust any straps. 
Deputies checked on Durrah several times, but no medical care was provided. They didn’t call for an ambulance until staff discovered the 35-year-old unconscious.
A Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation report of the incident, which took 15 months to complete, cleared jail staff of criminal wrongdoing. 
“To this day, there has been no accountability,” Killmer said in a statement. “Campbell County imposed no discipline against anyone. The Durrah family’s lawsuit aims to force a reckoning, so that the County can no longer sweep Kenneth Durrah’s death under the rug and continue with business as usual.”
The lawsuit recounts the hours and minutes leading to Durrah’s death. It often mirrors jailhouse surveillance videos obtained by WyoFile and the Gillette News Record in 2024. 
At about 1:20 a.m., Dec. 1, 2022, inmates on Durrah’s cell block began flickering their lights on and off to attract deputies’ attention in response to Durrah’s complaints that he needed medical attention, the lawsuit recounts. Multiple inmates reported that Durrah had complained of breathing and heart problems and called for a medic. 
According to the complaint, Durrah had advised jail medical staff during his medical intake screening that he had a history of asthma. 
Deputies Robert Shirley, Mara Madrid, Jonathan Herman and Ryan Wells, as well as Sgt. Mara Donathon — all of whom are named as defendants in the complaint — responded to Durrah’s cell. 
Durrah collapsed when deputies opened the door, clutching at his chest and telling them that his “heart hurt.” Shirley observed that Durrah’s “fists were repeatedly clenching and his toes were repeatedly curling,” according to the complaint, which includes images of the unfolding incident. The deputies determined that Durrah had “an elevated [heart rate] and high blood pressure.” 
No nurses or other medical staff were working in the jail at the time of this incident, according to the complaint. The county’s “affirmative and conscious decision” not to provide nighttime medical staff puts “inmates at risk of receiving inadequate medical care at night,” the complaint states. 
Donathon told deputies to take Durrah to the jail’s booking area and called outside medics to evaluate him. Another defendant, Deputy Stephanie Quinones, was processing an incoming inmate when Durrah arrived. She later told investigators that the man “was so out of breath that it looked like ‘he just ran five miles.’” Durrah vomited while he waited for medical help, the complaint states. 
The medics asked Durrah to try to calm down so that he could breathe regularly, and Durrah complied. They confirmed that Durrah’s blood pressure and heart rate were high, and Durrah told them he had a history of asthma. But the medics cleared him to remain in the jail. 
“As a matter of consistent practice and policy, Defendant Campbell County did not staff its jail with any medical providers or other medical staff during the relevant timeframe, which was late evening and early morning hours,” the complaint states. “There was not so much as a nurse on duty to observe Mr. Durrah once the medical responders departed.” 
Donathon ordered Durrah to be placed in a holding cell so that deputies could monitor him until nursing staff arrived for work in the morning, according to the complaint. Durrah “continued to report that it was difficult for him to breathe” and “repeatedly requested water.” 
Later, Wells and Quinones saw through Durrah’s cell door window “a small white object” in Durrah’s mouth. As Wells watched, Durrah “ripped open the bag with his hands and teeth and began to swallow the contents.” Wells “believed the bag contained drugs,” and Durrah indicated that he had swallowed some of the contents, the suit claims. 
The complaint states the bag contained methamphetamine, and that Durrah showed several symptoms of ingesting methamphetamine “over the course of the lengthy uses of force which the CCSO deputies would soon inflict upon him.” 
Wells called for Durrah’s cell door to be opened, and Donathon “suggested that the deputies should get Narcan ready.” 
“The fact that Defendant Donathon suggested the use of Narcan demonstrates that she was aware of the medical risks attendant to Mr. Durrah’s ingestion of a dangerous quantity of drugs, and that this was a serious medical issue,” the complaint states. 
None of the deputies “administered Narcan or took any other action to mitigate the effects of a potential drug overdose,” according to the complaint. Nor did they call for medical help. “Instead, when the cell door opened, Defendant Wells ran into the cell to initiate a violent, reckless, and patently excessive use of force against Mr. Durrah.” 
Wells stuck his fingers into Durrah’s mouth “to try to remove the bag of drugs.” Quinones entered after and “also went hands-on” with Durrah. “Terrified and confused, Mr. Durrah first huddled in a corner of the cell, then ran out the cell’s open door into the jail’s booking area,” where Wells tackled him, the complaint states. 
Prone restraint
Wells told Durrah to roll over. Durrah complied, turning onto his stomach. The deputies then put their knees on Durrah and leaned their body weight on him, “pushing him to a state of extreme physical exertion while substantially impairing his ability to respirate,” the complaint states.  
Deputies “could and should have physically controlled” Durrah without using this “dangerous” prone position, which is known to inhibit breathing, the complaint states. “Because of his known drug ingestion, he obviously needed medical help, rather than additional strain being forced upon him by the Defendants.” 
Wells and Quinones used their knees and hands to put pressure on Durrah’s back, leg and arms, the complaint describes. Donathon then “joined in,” putting her knee on Durrah’s “upper back and neck and leaning on him with her full body weight.” As they applied pressure, Durrah “cried out in a choppy, labored voice: ‘I can’t breathe!’” according to the suit. Surveillance video also captured Durrah saying he couldn’t breathe. 
Wells then “reinitiated use of force in earnest, clambering onto Mr. Durrah’s back and wrapping a forearm around Mr. Durrah’s neck,” after which he “wrenched” Durrah backward so that he was face-up, the complaint continues. Durrah “screamed in pain and terror” as Wells “applied pressure” to his neck and covered Durrah’s “mouth with his right arm, further impairing his ability to breathe.” 
Quinones “climbed on top” of Durrah, according to the complaint. Donathon “stood and moved” to Durrah’s lower body, then took out her Orcutt Police Nunchaku — sticks connected with a cord that can be used for restraint — and used it on Durrah’s right ankle. 
Campbell County Sheriff’s Detention Officer Samuel Boyles kneels over Kenneth Durrah’s back with Officer Robert Shirley at his feet, Officer Stephanie Quinones on his right side and Officer Ryan Wells at his head. (screenshot of Campbell County Detention Center video)
“All of the Defendant law enforcement officers were observing the excessive force applied to Mr. Durrah, and despite a legal obligation to intervene to prevent application of excessive force on a suspect, each of these named defendants failed to intervene to terminate the constitutional violation,” the lawsuit states. 
Another deputy, Samuel Boyles, “ran to join the overwhelming concerted use of force.” The deputies and sergeant rolled Durrah to his stomach again. Wells put both his hands on Durrah’s upper back, then put his knee on Durrah’s head, “grinding it into the concrete floor.” 
The lawsuit states Quinones held Durrah’s legs down with her body weight. Donathon continued to pin Durrah’s legs. Boyles put both knees on Durrah’s back. They held Durrah in this position for over a minute as they handcuffed him. Shirley arrived and replaced Donathon to pin Durrah’s feet. 
“Throughout the great majority of this period, Mr. Durrah was immobile and compliant; at that point, it required no significant exertion by the deputies to hold him,” the complaint states, noting that one of the deputies told Durrah not to move his leg, to which Durrah responded, “Yes, sir.” Durrah also asked the deputies to give him Narcan, according to the complaint. Video footage also shows him asking for Narcan. 
“Mr. Durrah was subdued and incapacitated by that time, but the force continued,” the complaint states. “Defendants handcuffed Mr. Durrah
behind his back as they crushed him.” 
Rather than putting Durrah in a “recovery position” — a position that allows someone to breathe freely — deputies carried Durrah to another holding cell and cut off his clothes while continuing to put pressure on him in a prone position. Quinones and Shirley crossed Durrah’s legs and “forced them up toward his back,” putting his body into a “dangerous ‘hog-tie’ position by placing increased pressure on his chest, further depriving him of breath.” 
Durrah “began to squirm” beneath the deputies in “severe pain and rising panic.” He told the deputies repeatedly that “he was struggling to breathe and begged them to let up the pressure on his back.” 
Restraint chair
As the deputies continued to apply pressure to Durrah, Donathon retrieved the restraint chair, which is equipped with straps to prevent the use of limbs. 
As the deputies strapped Durrah into the chair, Madrid used a “pain-compliance hold” near Durrah’s jaw, “causing even more pain and placing even greater stress on his already overtaxed system.” Though Durrah was secured in the chair and “offering no resistance whatsoever,” Shirley, Boyles and Wells “aggressively and intentionally overtightened” the straps across Durrah’s chest and waist, the complaint alleges. Wells “yanked hard on the straps until he physically could not make them any tighter.” According to the complaint, Shirley told investigators that it was “the tightest that he had ever seen the straps on the restraint chair.” 
Boyles wheeled Durrah, who was “grimacing in agony,” into another holding cell, the complaint describes. He left the door open so that Durrah could be seen and heard by deputies in the booking area. Durrah “repeatedly told the deputies that the restraint chair was too tight and that he could not breathe,” but they “ignored him.” The deputies didn’t call for medical services to assess Durrah. 
As Durrah “cried out in pain and begged for help,” Wells, Quinones and Donathon “joked and laughed” with Cpl. Marlene Sharpe “only a few feet away,” according to the complaint. Sharpe said she had heard about “the naked black guy trying to escape.” Wells “put on a high false voice and mocked Mr. Durrah’s pleas for medical help: ‘Give me Narcan!’” 
Quinones, the suit alleges, “joined in on the act and mockingly caricatured Mr. Durrah’s desperate explanations that he was struggling to breathe: ‘I can’t breathe, I can’t breathe.’” 
According to the lawsuit, Sharpe later told investigators that she told deputies to check Durrah out of concern for his medical condition after learning about the uses of force against him and his ingesting drugs. But Sharpe didn’t tell deputies to check Durrah for “nearly half an hour” after she had learned of this, when Durrah “had already become unresponsive.” 
Wells later entered the cell to check Durrah, who was unresponsive. But Wells still didn’t call for medical help, according to the complaint. “Instead, and inexplicably, Defendant Wells gave Defendant Donathon a thumbs-up and reported that Mr. Durrah was breathing.” Wells told Sharpe that Durrah “was asleep.” 
When Wells returned later, he “repeatedly called” Durrah’s name “to no response.” Wells told Donathon to call an ambulance. Wells, Boyles and Shirley removed Durrah from the restraint chair and attempted to perform CPR. Boyles and Shirley “were plainly unfamiliar with CPR technique and required direction from Corporal Sharpe to perform CPR after initially bungling their own CPR efforts,” the complaint states. Medics rushed Durrah by ambulance to the Campbell County Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. 
Civil rights
Durrah’s family alleges the deputies and Campbell County violated his Fourth, Eighth and 14th Amendment rights — to be free from excessive force and deliberate indifference to his medical needs, and to receive adequate medical care while in the jail’s custody. 
He was “in obvious and serious need of immediate medical care” from the moment he ingested methamphetamine, the complaint states. The force that deputies subsequently used against Durrah was “significantly disproportionate to any legitimate law enforcement need.” 
Video shows Campbell County Detention Center deputies kneeling over Kenneth Durrah’s back and head for a minute before they moved him and pinned him on his belly again for five minutes. (screenshot of Campbell County Detention Center video) 
The county’s policy directed employees to notify medical professionals when using the restraint chair, but the deputies didn’t get medical assistance for Durrah after he was put in the device. The policies also tell officers to refrain from putting people in positions that would significantly restrict their breathing and warn that weight “such as officers sitting or kneeling” on someone can cause asphyxia. 
“Campbell County and the Sheriff’s Office inadequately trained its detention staff on the meaning and methods of compliance with policies ostensibly designed to protect detainees’ safety and their constitutional rights,” the complaint states. The sheriff’s office didn’t undertake its own investigation into the deputies’ conduct and compliance with jail policies, according to the complaint, and none of the deputies were placed on administrative leave as the department’s policy requires after an officer’s use of force causes death. 
Durrah’s family is asking for punitive damages, attorney’s fees and compensation for emotional distress, funeral expenses and “other pain and suffering.”

title: Doctor fights medical board’s findings of fraud in denying him a license
description: A physician accused of failing to report past sanctions imposed in other states is taking the Iowa Board of Medicine to court over its refusal to issue him a license. According to board records, Dr. Adrian Gollas of Sioux City is a physician specializing in anesthesiology who in 2023 submitted an application for a license […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Medicine regulates the state's medical profession as part of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. (Photo by Getty Images, board seal courtesy the State of Iowa) A physician accused of failing to report past sanctions imposed in other states is taking the Iowa Board of Medicine to court over its refusal to issue him a license.
According to board records, Dr. Adrian Gollas of Sioux City is a physician specializing in anesthesiology who in 2023 submitted an application for a license to practice in Iowa. The board later determined that three answers Gollas provided in his application were incorrect.
Board records indicate Gollas attributes the incorrect answers to his use of a third-party professional licensing service to assist with the application process. The false answers were the result of errors and inadvertence on the part of the service, he alleges.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Board of Medicine records show the false answers were tied to questions about whether Gollas had ever been asked to repeat, or had been terminated from, an internship, residency or fellowship; whether he’d ever taken a leave of absence from medical school, a residency or a fellowship, and whether any other jurisdiction had filed disciplinary charges against him or imposed sanctions.
According to the board, Gollas was once removed from a residency program for failure to renew an expired work permit and, separately, was not allowed to continue his training for alleged performance and behavioral issues. The board alleges he also took a leave of absence at one point, and that both the Texas and New Mexico medical boards took action against him in the past for allegedly “mispresenting facts to them.”
An Iowa Board of Medicine hearing on Gollas’ application was held in June 2026, and in July 2026, the board denied Gollas a license, concluding he had committed fraud in attempting to procure an Iowa license. Prior to the hearing, Gollas allegedly indicated an Iowa medical provider — unnamed in the board’s public filings — was willing to hire him pending the approval of his license application.
Gollas recently filed a petition in Polk County District Court, seeking judicial review of the Board of Medicine’s decision, asserting the evidence does not establish that he intentionally provided false information or acted with reckless disregard for the truth.
The petition seeks a court order reversing the board’s decision to deny Gollas a license.
The board has yet to file a response to Gollas’ petition, but in its July decision the board stated that Gollas “blaming his erroneous answers on a third-party vendor assisting him in filling out his application may explain what happened but it is not a legal defense.”
Citing what it called Gollas’ “pattern of untruthful answers” to not only the Iowa Board of Medicine but also other regulatory bodies, the Iowa board stated in its decision: “While Dr. Gollas may have a strong history of patient care and has provided much assistance to his family and community, this cannot outweigh the pattern of untruthful answers, which frankly calls into question either his honesty – which is a core trait demanded of doctors – or his ability to be attentive to details, which is also a core trait expected of doctors.”
Court records indicate Gollas’ past disciplinary issues stem from decisions at the University of Texas Health Science Center where his work performance, treatment of fellow residents, and episodes of inappropriate behavior were cited by the school as reasons for terminating his residency there.
New Mexico Medical Board records state that Gollas “later filed an unsuccessful lawsuit against the University of Texas, claiming that the university retaliated against him by revoking his appointment for the third year of his residency.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Gollas for comment.

title: Food landscape assessment reveals South Dakota’s gaps in access, affordability and assistance
description: In a survey weighted toward South Dakotans most likely to experience food insecurity, 30% indicated they were skipping meals to stay within their budget, according to the recently released South Dakota Food Landscape Assessment. The assessment is the first of its kind in the state, identifying gaps in food affordability, access, assistance, availability and[...]
text:
Vegetables and lettuces at a grocery store in Michigan. A summer of food recalls, including the record-shattering cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce that has sickened thousands, has raised many Americans’ fears of contracting a foodborne illness. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)In a survey weighted toward South Dakotans most likely to experience food insecurity, 30% indicated they were skipping meals to stay within their budget, according to the recently released South Dakota Food Landscape Assessment.
The assessment is the first of its kind in the state, identifying gaps in food affordability, access, assistance, availability and quality statewide. The information will give policymakers, lawmakers, researchers and community organizers a shared foundation to improve programs and drive policy changes, said Jennifer Folliard, principal consultant at Health and Nutrition First and coordinator for the South Dakota Healthy Nutrition Collaborative.
With the skipped meals and affordability information in hand, for example, the report recommends introducing produce prescriptions in South Dakota — a program that lets healthcare providers “prescribe” fruits and vegetables, redeemable at grocery stores or farmers markets. Other states have funded similar programs through Medicaid waivers, which allow states to use federal health insurance dollars in new ways, or through nonprofit funding.
 

 Community conversations

The South Dakota Healthy Nutrition Collaborative will host five community conversations about the South Dakota Food Landscape assessment findings:

5:30 p.m. on Sept. 16 at the Drifters Event Center in Fort Pierre.
5:30 p.m. on Sept. 17 at the Oyate Teca Project in Kyle.
5:30 p.m. on Sept. 18 at the Journey Museum in Rapid City.
5:30 p.m. on Sept. 23 at Avera St. Lukes in Aberdeen.
5:30 p.m. on Sept. 24 at the University of South Dakota Sioux Falls campus.




The idea was discussed during the latest legislative session, Folliard said, when lawmakers approved a law that requires the state Department of Social Services to seek a waiver to ban soft drinks from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The state submitted its waiver request on Monday.
“When we were talking about SNAP restrictions, we also tried to raise the idea that if you restrict, it’s also good to incentivize healthy food,” Folliard said. “I think we can have those conversations next session a little bit more based on the data that came from this report.”
The state Department of Health has already designated child food sufficiency as a priority through its maternal and child health programs, providing momentum for the collaborative’s work, Folliard said.
The longer-term goal is a full food systems plan — a coordinated, statewide strategy for how food is grown, distributed and accessed, especially during times of economic stress. The collaborative is seeking funding to create the plan. 
The assessment was produced through a partnership with the state Department of Health, Avera Research Institute, University of South Dakota’s Center for Prevention of Child Maltreatment, and the South Dakota Healthy Nutrition Collaborative. The collaborative brings together 40 organizations, including the state departments of Health, Human Services and Social Services.
More than 500 people participated in the assessment survey — including 217 community members (weighted toward South Dakotans most at risk of food insecurity based on age, geography and tribal affiliation) and 295 people involved in the food system, in fields such as healthcare, education, policy, etc. The assessment also included one-on-one interviews and focus groups.
Food security information is often scattered across agencies and organizations, Folliard said, making it hard for anyone to see the full picture.
“Food is at the base of all health,” said Folliard, who co-authored the assessment. “It’s everywhere, so no one’s taking ownership of it. The organizations that came together for this assessment recognized that we all have to play a part in figuring this out together.”
South Dakota seeks to ban use of food assistance for soda purchases as court ruling clouds issue

In South Dakota, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1 in 8 people and 1 in 5 children have limited or uncertain access to enough food, and 1 in 8 residents eat enough fruits and vegetables each day. 
Those gaps don’t just affect individual health — they can drive up healthcare costs, strain schools and social services, and limit economic opportunity across the state, the assessment said.
In addition to affordability, the assessment included findings in key areas of food security and the state’s food system, including:

Assistance: About 70,000 South Dakotans rely on the federal-state Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and income cutoffs create a “benefits cliff” where earning slightly more can cost a family nearly $1,000 in monthly food assistance.
Access: 13 counties have food insecurity rates above the national average and 43 counties are considered food swamps, which are areas where dollar stores and convenience stores outnumber grocery stores.
Availability: 359 of South Dakota’s 28,299 farms are specialty operations growing the fruits, vegetables and whole foods that improve nutrition security.

The assessment’s data extends beyond the published report. The state Department of Health recently launched an interactive dashboard because of the assessment, drawing on several datasets — dollar-store counts, diabetes rates, farm-to-school participation and SNAP vendor locations — that the department will update periodically.
That information gives local governments, community organizations and researchers the ability to examine their specific county and identify where targeted action is most needed, said Christine Hockett, director of community research at Avera Research Institute and a University of South Dakota associate professor who co-authored the assessment.
“When reports like these are published, a lot of times it happens once and then it’s like, ‘OK, what happens now?’ There’s no sustainability plan,” Hockett said. “As we were harmonizing and bringing the data together, we were doing it with the idea that we would ultimately share this with the Department of Health to make it accessible to everybody.”

name: VTDigger
title: UVM Medical Center quietly changed its policy for patient observation. Some staff are worried about patient safety.
description:
Staff unions sent the hospital a cease and desist letter regarding the change in practice, which comes as the hospital makes rapid strides to cut expenses. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM Medical Center quietly changed its policy for patient observation. Some staff are worried about patient safety..
text:
The University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington on November 2020. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
In June, UVM Medical Center quietly rolled out a new policy dictating how its staff watch over patients who are at risk of hurting themselves while they’re in the hospital. 
Sitters, or clinical patient safety attendants — CPSAs — stay with patients who need supervision. Patients who might fall, wander or pull out IVs are often assigned sitters, as are those who are at highly suicidal or epileptic. Often, licensed nursing assistants fill this role, too. 
But, a new hospital policy limits LNAs from filling the role, Annie Mackin spokesperson for UVMMC told VTDigger.
The change is to keep LNAs staffed on more “direct” patient care needs, Mackin wrote. 
Instead, the hospital is prioritizing remote patient monitoring — essentially, a video monitor on wheels connected to a remote observer watching many patients at once — or dispatching designated observation staff, not LNAs, when necessary. 
But staff are concerned about the gaps left by that system.
“There have been patients that I personally thought, ‘I don’t feel safe having this patient in my assignment without a CPSA with them,’ ” Saer McCliment, an LNA at the medical center, told VTDigger. 
Previously, an LNA could fill in as a sitter as part of their regular duties, which are under the supervision of a nurse and include much of a patient’s daily living care. 
“Lately, not only has that really not been available, but we’ve been told that there are only allowed to be a specific number of CPSAs working in the hospital at any one time,” McCliment said. 
The hospital now staffs 17 CSPAs each shift for all 14 inpatient units and the emergency department, according to Brett Rhodes, another UVMMC LNA. His floor alone can need up to five CSPAs at a given time, he said.
Remote monitoring doesn’t work for many of the patients who need it, they said, adding that many of the patients at risk of pulling out IVs or wandering off are experiencing psychosis or dementia. Hearing a disembodied voice through a remote monitor’s video screen can exacerbate those patients’ paranoia and confusion. 
“That’s just not safe or fair for them,” McCliment said.  
On Aug. 20, representatives from two of the UVM Health network’s labor unions sent a cease and desist letter to the network’s labor relations director, formally requesting the hospital pause the June changes to its observation policy. The change impedes the bargaining for new contracts both unions have been undergoing since April, the letter stated. The support staff union, which includes LNAs, has been working on an expired contract since mid-August.
The unions’ letter also detailed that if an LNA is pulled from their regular duties to provide patient observation, the hospital has not been able to fill in with additional LNAs to cover their tasks, resulting in a unit being short staffed 
The authors also wrote that nurses’ input regarding remote observation and sitter practices are “reportedly no longer being appropriately considered and, in some cases, are being disregarded.” 
Mackin stressed that the hospital is still assigning in-person sitters for some very high-risk patients. “Patient safety remains our top priority, and making workforce roles clear helps us use our resources efficiently while continuing to provide high-quality, affordable care,” she wrote.
The changes come as part of a sweeping series of expense cuts the UVM Health network, the medical center’s parent organization, is pushing in order to make ends meet as it faces dramatic drops in revenue largely due to a reduction in what it charges the state’s largest private insurer BlueCross BlueShield and a law prohibiting big markups on the price of pharmaceutical drugs.
The network expects to lose more than $14 million across the system in the coming fiscal year, which begins Oct. 1, according to its August budget presentation to the Green Mountain Care Board. UVM Medical Center is expected to operate at a $43 million loss. 
Already, the network has proposed $140 million in cuts to expenses for the coming fiscal year, and still it needs to make more.

READ MORE

“We do recognize that current challenges may require us to implement operational changes more quickly and more frequently than employees and unions have historically experienced. We value the unions’ partnership as we navigate these challenges while recognizing the pace of change may be difficult at times for staff,” Mackin wrote in a statement. She added that the changes are within UVM Health’s “contractual authority to adjust staffing assignments.” 
Staff worry that patients are facing the consequences of this change. 
Rhodes said he knew of five incidents in which patient safety had been compromised because patients didn’t have an appropriate sitter. He worried that the lack of sitters means patients in the ICU may be overly sedated in order to avoid worse complications. 
“This would never have been a problem before they instituted that policy,” he said. “They are rolling the dice on safety.”
Much of what LNAs do inherently guards against many basic safety risks, according to McCliment.
“We help patients get up to the bathroom. We help them bathe and dress. We help them eat all their meals and take vital signs, get ready for bed. We help them move around safely in bed and out of the bed in the hospital,” they said. “We’re the people that are physically in the room with the patients the most.”
Patients’ needs don’t decrease just because there are fewer staff, they said.
“Someone who needs to go to the bathroom won’t wait 15 minutes for you,” McCliment said. “They just get up and go. And if they need help walking, or if they’re a fall risk, they can fall, which is extremely serious.”

title: Harvest season nears in Iowa; Farm Rescue taking applications
description: Less than 10% of Iowa corn acres have reached the mature stage as of the latest crop progress and condition report, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture anticipates some reports of  harvested acres to appear in the next weekly report.  According to the USDA report for the Aug. 24 through Aug. 31 reporting period, 6% […]
text:
Corn grows along west-bound U.S. 80 in Iowa Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Less than 10% of Iowa corn acres have reached the mature stage as of the latest crop progress and condition report, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture anticipates some reports of  harvested acres to appear in the next weekly report. 

According to the USDA report for the Aug. 24 through Aug. 31 reporting period, 6% of Iowa corn acres had reached maturity, which is 2 percentage points behind the 2025 and five-year average pace. 
Corn that has reached the dent stage, at 68%, however, is significantly higher than last year and the 5-year average, which the report shows at 60% and 62% respectively. Nearly all corn acres, 94%, have reached the dough stage as of the latest report. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa’s corn crop continues to rate well with 77% marked good to excellent for the reporting period. Soybeans also rated 77% good to excellent condition. 
A scant number of soybean acres was reported to be dropping leaves during the reporting period and 93% of the crop was reported to be setting pods, which is slightly behind last years pace and the five-year average. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said in a news release that the warm weather expected through the rest of the coming week will “continue to push crop development.” 
State Climatologist Justin Glisan said that while rain fell across most of the state during the reporting period, it wasn’t much. Most weather stations reported below normal amounts of precipitation, and the statewide average for the week was 0.32 inch, while the normal precipitation for the period is 0.91 inch. 
Soil moisture conditions did not change much from the week prior. Both topsoil and subsoil rate as 67% adequate moisture. 
The statewide average temperature for the week, at 70.1 degrees Fahrenheit, was less than 1 degree above the normal, according to Glisan.
Farm Rescue support during harvest
The volunteer organization, Farm Rescue, is accepting applications and referrals for free harvest assistance to farmers and farm families in need this season. 
The organization started in South Dakota in 2005 to help farmers and their families get crops out of the field when major illnesses, injuries or natural disasters make normal harvest impossible. 
Farm Rescue uses volunteers, donors and business partners to help farmers with equipment and “manpower” to get “time sensitive” farm chores done.
Shari Rogge-Fidler, the executive director of Farm Rescue, said in a statement that Farm Rescue can “help carry the load” for families facing crisis. 
“In rural communities, neighbors have always looked out for one another, but during harvest, those same neighbors are often working long days to bring in their own crops,” Rogge-Fidler said. “That’s where Farm Rescue can step in.” 
The service is available in Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Wisconsin, Montana and Kentucky. Farmers, neighbors, ag professionals and community members are encouraged to refer families in need of harvest assistance to Farm Rescue. Families can also apply directly for assistance.

title: US Supreme Court lets Trump move ahead with his White House ballroom project
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump does not have to follow a lower court order to stop aboveground construction on his $400 million East Wing ballroom, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday in a 5-4 decision, all but guaranteeing work on the new complex will continue to accelerate.In an opinion from the conservative super-majority, the justices wrote that historic preservationists who sued to stop the project likely do not have standing and that the administration would be irreparably harmed by halting the construction.National security officials, including several Cabinet members, the majority justices wrote, issued statements in the case “attesting to national security and other harms that would likely arise from enjoining a ‘single, coherent’ project that cannot be readily cleaved into distinct below- and above-ground pieces.”“The Secretary of the Army, for example, represents that ‘[t]he height and mass’ of the planned above-ground ballroom are ‘crucial’ to shield the planned underground military installation ‘from kinetic impacts,’ and that, without such height and mass, ‘engineers would need to dig impractically deep,’” according to the unsigned opinion.The justices wrote the stay is in effect pending a “timely” petition from the Trump administration to ask the high court to take the case this upcoming term, also known as granting a writ of certiorari. Monday’s opinion came from what’s known as the emergency docket, which provides expedited decisions without full oral arguments.“Should certiorari be denied, this stay shall terminate automatically. In the event certiorari is granted, the stay shall terminate upon the sending down of the judgment of this Court,” the justices wrote.Trump triumphantTrump wrote on his platform Truth Social that he’s “pleased to report that the United States Supreme Court has just ruled in favor of the Ballroom/Military Complex being built without any further contingency, doubt, or threat. We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.”Trump added he expects the “magnificent” project to be completed by the summer of 2028 and that it is “totally funded by Great Patriots and Corporations and, therefore, is a Gift — At no cost to the American Taxpayer.”The administration has maintained in court filings that the East Wing project is paid for by private donations.Trump continued: “The Project, despite the baseless lawsuit brought by the so-called National Trust for Historic Preservation of the United States, which is not in any way affiliated with the United States Government, is under budget and ahead of schedule.”The National Trust for Historic Preservation, which brought the suit, did not immediately respond for comment. The private nonprofit was chartered by Congress in 1949 to encourage the protection of historic sites.Roberts disagreesIn a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts and liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote the construction is “likely unlawful” because Congress did not approve the changes to the White House grounds, which sit on federal park land.“Today’s decision is no victory for the separation of powers,” Roberts wrote in the dissenting opinion.The administration filed to the court’s emergency docket Aug. 13 asking the justices to block the lower court’s order, after a panel of federal appeals judges upheld it in a split decision a week prior.Roberts granted a weeklong temporary stay on the lower court’s order while the justices took more time to consider the arguments.The Trump administration maintained the planned 90,000-square-foot facility slated for where the White House East Wing used to stand will reach deep underground and will seat approximately 1,000 guests in an aboveground ballroom that is vital to national security. Trump demolished the East Wing in October 2025.Officials told the Supreme Court justices in their stay application that as of mid-August, the project was already 65% complete, with a concrete-and-steel “superstructure” reaching five stories underground and 70 feet high, occupying nearly 50,000 square feet. Over the past four months, workers on a 250-person crew had been operating 20 hours a day, seven days a week, “to keep the Project ahead of schedule and under budget,” U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote, adding that $200 million has been spent or committed to date, and has been “shouldered by private donations.”

title: Northwest Arkansas hospital becomes latest site for state’s maternal health program
description: A program aimed at supporting high-risk pregnancies has expanded to Mercy Hospital Northwest Arkansas, Department of Human Services officials announced Monday.  The Maternal Life360 program provides low-income pregnant women with home visits from trained community outreach workers through a child’s second birthday. The program is part of the state’s efforts[...]
text:
Elizabeth Pitman, director of the Arkansas Department of Human Services’ Division of Medical Services, speaks at a Maternal Life 360 program blessing and launch at Mercy Hospital Northwest Arkansas in Rogers on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)A program aimed at supporting high-risk pregnancies has expanded to Mercy Hospital Northwest Arkansas, Department of Human Services officials announced Monday. 
The Maternal Life360 program provides low-income pregnant women with home visits from trained community outreach workers through a child’s second birthday. The program is part of the state’s efforts to address poor maternal outcomes in Arkansas, a state with some of the nation’s highest maternal and infant mortality rates.
Drive time to Arkansas hospitals for labor and delivery getting longer, report shows

“The need has never been greater in the state of Arkansas,” Whitney Tolbert, Mercy Northwest Arkansas’ vice president of women’s and children’s services, said during a program blessing and launch celebration Monday. 
To be eligible, participants must be enrolled in Medicaid or the state’s Medicaid expansion program, have a high-risk pregnancy diagnosis and live in a Life360 service area, according to the Department of Human Services. They also must not be receiving any state or federally funded home-visiting services.
Mercy Northwest Arkansas is partnering with Springdale-based nonprofit Family Network to deliver services, which include education on healthy pregnancy, postpartum recovery and newborn care, according to a press release. 
Family Network has provided in-home services in the region for more than 25 years, “a very powerful intervention” that breaks down many barriers, Executive Director Audrey Zavaleta said. 
“Because the home visitors, community outreach workers, are literally going into the home, sitting on moms’ couches, talking to them as a friend,” Zavaleta said. “They’re building that trusting relationship.”
Family Network Executive Director Audrey Zavaleta speaks at a Maternal Life 360 program blessing and launch at Mercy Hospital Northwest Arkansas in Rogers on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
Participants also receive assistance accessing transportation, community resources, diapers and wipes, parent support groups and other services available in English, Spanish and Marshallese, according to the release. 
“We know this model works, and so being able to expand it to other areas of the state through this program, that’s what we’re here for,” said Elizabeth Pitman, director of the Department of Human Services’ Division of Medical Services, which manages the state’s Medicaid program.
Mercy Northwest Arkansas is the fourth location for the program in operation. A fifth had been offered through White River Health in Batesville, but that program closed in June, officials said. Baptist Health operates programs in Little Rock and North Little Rock, and St. Bernards offers a program in Jonesboro.
The state intends to continue expanding the program, DHS officials said.
