name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ joins feds in lawsuit targeting Amazon over ad pricing
description: The lawsuit alleges Amazon for years inflated auction prices that businesses pay to place ads in its storefront, a claim Amazon denied.
text:
The lawsuit alleges Amazon for years inflated auction prices that businesses pay to place ads in its storefront, a claim Amazon denied. (Photo courtesy of Edwin J. Torres/New Jersey Governor's Office)New Jersey, 21 other states, and the Federal Trade Commission sued Amazon Monday, alleging the e-commerce giant had for years overcharged businesses for product advertisements placed in search results on its storefront.
Amazon rigged auctions it used to set prices for advertisement space on America’s largest online retailer, overcharging more than 500,000 businesses for more than $20 billion, the suit alleges.
“For years, Amazon has been misrepresenting how it sets the prices to advertise on the most coveted real estate on its website. It promised competitive auctions to set prices and then quietly replaced those results with inflated prices designed to pad its own profits,” New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport said in a statement.
Amazon in a statement said regulators had drawn their case from a small number of misleading emails and deprecated instructional videos and guides that it said did not fully explain how its ad sales worked.
“The FTC cherry-picked a small number of materials, such as a few online educational videos and training content that contained older or simplified examples about how our auctions are run, which were missed when we audited our materials as part of that initial update,” the company said in a statement posted to its website.
Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson said in a statement that the impact of the claims in the lawsuit are “staggering.”
“Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices. These higher costs were largely passed on to American consumers. The FTC under President Trump won’t allow this deception to continue,” Ferguson said.
The lawsuit alleges that Amazon had misrepresented pricing in the second-price auctions it purported to use to sell ad space. In second-price auctions, the winning bidder pays the smallest amount more than the runner-up, rather than their own bid.
But in 2019 the company began adding an undisclosed surcharge to auction prices and also used invented bidders to artificially inflate prices, the lawsuit alleges, citing internal documents and an Amazon senior scientist.
Amazon did not appear to deny using surcharges or invented bidders to boost auction prices but said it did not select winners based on the highest bid.
“The mean winning advertiser’s bid is typically about the 128th bid by amount. This means the winning advertisers’ cost is almost always lower than if we had selected ads on bid alone,” it said in the statement.

title: Leg amputation and injuries at Waterloo care facility trigger $53,750 in fines
description: For the third time in three months, an Iowa nursing home has been fined for resident injuries that include broken bones and gangrene. Between June 16, 2026, and Aug. 6, 2026, the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals investigated 14 complaints at Ravenwood Specialty Care, a 176-bed care facility in Waterloo, and imposed $53,750 in […]
text:
Ravenwood Specialty Care, a 176-bed care facility in Waterloo. (Photo via Google Earth)For the third time in three months, an Iowa nursing home has been fined for resident injuries that include broken bones and gangrene.
Between June 16, 2026, and Aug. 6, 2026, the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals investigated 14 complaints at Ravenwood Specialty Care, a 176-bed care facility in Waterloo, and imposed $53,750 in fines.
The first of the fines was imposed on June 16, when DIAL fined Ravenwood $7,750 for failing to assess and treat a male resident’s foot wound, which led to the man’s lower leg being amputated.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the state inspectors, a cognitively intact male resident who had lived at the facility since 2024 developed an open sore on his right foot in February 2026. By April 10, the foot was diagnosed with necrotic, dead tissue and was described by a foot care specialist as “very painful.” One toe was amputated at the time.
The wound continued to worsen and on April 27, another toe was amputated. By May 1, the resident was considered to be at high risk of a below-the-knee leg amputation.
On May 17, the resident was transferred to a hospital emergency room and diagnosed with sepsis, which is a  life-threatening infection, acute kidney failure and septic shock. Hospital staff reported the resident’s “foot appeared necrotic (due to) dead tissue,” with an “obvious gangrenous infection,” according to state inspectors.
The wound had split completely open, resulting in exposed bone, the inspectors reported. A below-the-knee amputation was performed the next day.
In addition to the $7,750 fine, the state also imposed a $6,250 fine for failing to intervene when another male resident of the home fell and broke his leg. The man reportedly told inspectors that he had fallen when he tried to walk to the bathroom without assistance, adding that he didn’t use his call light because “there’s no point in using it since it can take a couple of hours for staff to answer it.”
At the time of the June 16 inspection, the home was the focus of six separate complaints, three of which were substantiated.
More fines in June and August 
Two weeks after those fines were imposed, on June 30, the state imposed a fine of $5,750 for resident-safety violations, and then tripled that to $17,250 due to the recurring nature of the problem.
That penalty stemmed from an incident in which a female resident was hospitalized after a worker inadvertently injured the woman’s leg by improperly lowering the footrest of her recliner.
At the time, Ravenwood was the subject of four complaints, three of which were substantiated by inspectors.
On Aug. 6, inspectors returned to the home and imposed an additional $7,500 fine for resident-safety violations, which was then tripled to $22,500 due to the recurring nature of the problem. At that time, the home was the subject of six complaints, three of which were deemed substantiated.
The $22,500 penalty was tied to an incident involving a male resident who wandered from the facility sometime after midnight on July 29 — four days after his admission. The staff heard the door alarm sound but failed to perform a count of the residents, according to inspectors.
Inspectors reported that around 2:15 a.m., police spotted the man lying face down in the roadway next to the curb. The man was wearing socks and the top to a set of hospital scrubs and was taken by ambulance to a hospital. He was later treated for facial injuries, a large laceration to his head and a bruise on his forehead, inspectors reported.
According to the inspectors, the administrator at Ravenwood “acknowledged the facility did not have a door-alarm policy.” The missing-resident policy that had existed for the past eight years, since August 2018, lacked direction on how and when the staff was to respond to door alarms, inspectors reported.
It was in 2022 that Ravenwood was sued by the family of Michael Jensen, a former Wartburg College music instructor. According to the lawsuit, Jensen wandered away from Ravenwood, where he resided, on July 6, 2020. Four days later, inspectors reported, he was found in a ditch, submerged up to his chest in water. He was taken to a hospital and admitted to the intensive care unit for treatment of sepsis, hypothermia and  potential skeletal or heart-muscle damage. He remained in the hospital for 22 days.
DIAL subsequently fined Ravenwood $8,750 for the incident and because the home didn’t appeal the fine, the penalty was reduced to $5,687. The family’s lawsuit, which alleged negligence, breach of contract and dependent adult abuse, has been stayed pending the completion of arbitration proceedings scheduled for this month.
Ravenwood is operated by one of Iowa’s largest nursing home chains, Care Initiatives. The 176-bed home currently has a one-star rating of “much below average” on the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ website. CMS has imposed no federal penalties on the home during the past three years, according to the site.
In May 2025, the family of the late Mickey Neal sued the owners of Ravenwood, alleging negligence and wrongful death. The lawsuit claims Neal was admitted to Ravenwood on March 15, 2024, and that two weeks later, on April 3, 2024, the staff found him on the floor of his room, incontinent and bleeding from a head wound. He was then transferred to UnityPoint Allen Hospital, where he died on April 7, 2024.
A trial is scheduled for July 13, 2027.

name: VTDigger
title: Why are we spending $3 million on doctors who leave?
description:
Vermont is betting millions on a slow pipeline that loses half its doctors anyway, when a fix that works immediately is already sitting in a hospital budget filing.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Why are we spending $3 million on doctors who leave?.
text:
Dear Editor,
I truly appreciated Olivia Gieger’s recent article in VTDigger on the question of who pays for training Vermont’s doctors. It is a much-needed glimpse into a critical and sorely undercovered subject.
The memo — a Green Mountain Care Board filing on what it costs the University of Vermont Medical Center to train doctors — answers how much. It never asks how much per doctor, and these figures give it. Vermont spends $161 million per year training 320 residents and fellows at any given time. With a typical three-year program, about a third finish each year, and nearly half of those stay on, roughly 50 physicians retained annually. That works out to at least $3 million for every physician Vermont keeps, and longer programs push the number even higher: Surgery runs five years, not three.
Three million dollars would bring almost anyone here. It would then be our job to give them a reason to stay.
Vermont already knows how, and a hospital has published it. In its fiscal year 2026 budget narrative to the care board, Southwestern Vermont Medical Center lists 11 investments in nursing and concludes, “The areas of investment listed above enable SVMC to avoid nurse travelers.” In the same filing: “SVMC uses locum primary care physicians … when no other reasonable option exists.”
Same building, same town, same labor market. Opposite results, and the mechanism for the good one is already written down. Nobody has asked whether it transfers.
SVMC’s residency takes its first cohort in 2029, six a year, three years. The first physician finishes in 2032. At the retention rate reported here, about three stay annually thereafter. It’s a sound long-term instrument, but not an answer to a shortage we are living through now.

READ MORE

SVMC President & CEO Estevan Garcia says the program attracts experienced physicians who have a passion for teaching. He has it right, and backward. Residents arriving in 2029 need those physicians already here. 
Recruiting them isn’t a consequence of the residency; it is its precondition, and when successful, it works immediately.
Fred Schwacke
Bondville, Vt.

text:
The Florida Capitol building on March 11, 2026, as the legislative session neared its end. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Florida Disabilities Council Executive Director Valerie Breen announced her resignation Monday in an email, citing health concerns.
Florida Developmental Disabilities Council Executive Director Valerie Breen. (Via council.)
Former Agency for Persons with Disabilities Director and Tallahassee lobbyist Jim DeBeaugrine is serving as acting executive director until a permanent replacement for Breen is found.
Breen said she’s been away from work “dealing with a serious health matter.” She didn’t disclose any details but said between her health concerns and the scheduled end of her contract, she “has come to accept that  I  will not be able to return to my role as Executive Director before my contract concludes.”
“This is not how I envisioned ending my time with FDDC, and it is certainly not the way I would have chosen to say goodbye to an organization and community that have meant so much to me,” she said in the email.
She added that while she’s stepping away from the FDDC professionally, she is “not closing the door on the people who have been such an important part of my life.”
“I welcome cards, notes, emails, or other messages, although I may not always be able to respond right away. Please know that your thoughts and kindness are deeply appreciated,” she wrote.
The Florida Developmental Disabilities Council is an advisory board, established under the federal Developmental Disabilities and Bill of Rights Act. It is charged with helping create policies that improve the lives of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities as well as their families and other supports.
The council receives about $4 million annually in federal funding.
The 26 members of the council are appointed by the governor. The executive director works for the council.

name: National
title: Feds and 22 states sue Amazon, alleging deceptive advertising scheme
description: The Federal Trade Commission and attorneys general from 22 states sued Amazon Monday, claiming the online retail company used artificial bids to inflate costs for advertisers, bringing in tens of billions of dollars. The complaint alleges that Amazon used an “invented auction participant” to drive up prices for advertising placements and sponsored product sp[...]
text:
An Amazon warehouse near Newport, Delaware. The Federal Trade Commission and 22 states have sued Amazon over an alleged scheme to inflate advertising prices. (Photo by Jacob Owens/Spotlight Delaware)The Federal Trade Commission and attorneys general from 22 states sued Amazon Monday, claiming the online retail company used artificial bids to inflate costs for advertisers, bringing in tens of billions of dollars.
The complaint alleges that Amazon used an “invented auction participant” to drive up prices for advertising placements and sponsored product spots on its online store. The lawsuit quotes a former company employee who said the system allowed the company to charge prices “beyond what [can] be achieved through advertiser competition.”
“Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices,” FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement. “These higher costs were largely passed on to American consumers.”
The complaint says that Amazon has carried out the scheme for more than seven years, increasing prices for more than a million brands and sellers.
The FTC’s lawsuit was filed along with the attorneys general of Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont and Washington.
“As alleged, this is a textbook example of illegal behavior by a corporation which places profits above all else,” Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, a Democrat, said in a statement. “The ubiquity of Amazon in American society pushes small- and medium-sized businesses to engage with the Company in order to stay afloat.”
Per Neronha’s statement, the coalition is pursuing “civil penalties, restitution, costs and fees, and injunctive relief.”
In a blog post responding to the lawsuit, Amazon said that “the FTC’s claim fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate.” The company asserted that the average cost-per-click for sponsored product search ads remained flat adjusted for inflation from 2019 to 2024.
“After reviewing approximately 1.5 million pages spanning six years, the FTC leans on a handful of simplified communications to allege a companywide effort to deceive,” Amazon wrote in its blog. “That is patently false.”
The company claims its “soft reserve prices” allowed it to award advertisements to the most relevant bids, rather than the highest bid amount, while still charging the true market value of an ad placement.
The complaint was filed in U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. Amazon is headquartered in Seattle.
Amazon is the third-largest digital advertising business worldwide, according to CNBC, behind only Google and Meta, with more than $68 billion in ad revenue last year.
Last year, Amazon and the FTC agreed to a $2.5 billion settlement over separate allegations that the company deceptively enrolled customers in Prime subscriptions and made it difficult for them to cancel.
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org

title: Late nominations give Delaware voters more choices in November
description: Republicans added 10 candidates after Aug. 1, including eight during the final week before the deadline; Democrats added two By George D. Rotsch, Editor, Delaware LIVE DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s November ballot became considerably more competitive during August as the Republican Party nominated candidates for 10 offices that otherwise would have lacked a Repub[...]
text:
Republicans added 10 candidates after Aug. 1, including eight during the final week before the deadline; Democrats added two

By George D. Rotsch, Editor, Delaware LIVE
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s November ballot became considerably more competitive during August as the Republican Party nominated candidates for 10 offices that otherwise would have lacked a Republican contender.
Eight of those nominations were filed during the final week before Delaware’s Sept. 1 deadline for major parties to fill vacant ballot positions, according to the state Department of Elections.
The Democratic Party also made two late nominations, adding candidates for a Sussex County Senate seat and a New Castle County-area House district.
Brent Budge, chair of the Northern DEGOP region where many of these candidates are running and a newly added candidate himself, stated, “Most of the candidates came forward to give voters in these communities real options in November.  Incumbents and primary winners need to be challenged so voters can determine the future of their community.  That’s how democracy works.  These individuals are passionate about the neighborhoods and want to make a difference. They are knowledgeable about the community, local leaders, and understand the political process.”
“Contested elections allow voters to compare candidates, hear different positions and hold officeholders accountable,” concluded Burdge.

The Democratic Party nominated Harry S. Gold for the 20th Senate District on Aug. 25 and Tori Parker for the 11th Representative District on Aug. 28. Both are listed as qualified.
Several of the newly nominated Republicans will face Democratic incumbents or the winners of Democratic primaries. Graham, for example, is positioned to face the winner of the Democratic primary for attorney general, where incumbent Kathy Jennings is seeking another term.
Some November matchups will not be complete until Delaware holds its statewide primary Sept. 15.
A rarely used route to the ballot
Ordinarily, Democratic and Republican candidates file by the July deadline and advance through a primary if more than one candidate seeks the same party’s nomination.
State law provides another route when no candidate from a major party has filed for an office. Party officials may nominate someone to fill that ballot vacancy by submitting a certificate of nomination to the Department of Elections by Sept. 1.
The late nominees do not go through a primary because no other candidate from their party filed for the same office.
Delaware’s online candidate records indicate that this year’s Republican recruitment effort is unusually large. Eight Republican nominations were filed during the final week before the deadline. No Democratic or Republican organization matched that total in the state’s date-stamped candidate lists from 2010 through 2024.
The closest comparison came in 2016, when Republicans filed five candidates during the closing days of the nomination period. That year’s late additions included candidates for Wilmington offices and Kent County positions.
That makes this year’s group the largest final-week addition by either major party in at least 16 years. Records before 2010 available on the Department of Elections website do not contain filing dates, making a longer historical comparison difficult.
More candidates, but difficult campaigns
Late nomination comes with disadvantages.
Candidates entering near the deadline have little time to raise money, recruit volunteers, introduce themselves to voters and develop positions on complicated state issues. Some will be challenging incumbents who have spent years building name recognition and campaign organizations.
A name on the ballot, therefore, does not necessarily create a competitive campaign. The new candidates will still have to demonstrate that they are prepared to serve and capable of making a serious case to voters.
Their presence nevertheless prevents several races from being decided without a general-election contest.
Unopposed candidates can still be held accountable by the public, news organizations and members of their own party. But an opposing candidate creates a more direct test. Debates become possible. Policy differences become clearer. Voters can evaluate competing records and priorities before selecting who will represent them.
That is a basic feature of representative government: Elections work best when voters have meaningful choices.
Some candidates remain provisional
Several late nominees are currently listed as provisional by the Department of Elections.
Provisional status does not mean a candidate has been rejected. It generally means the state is reviewing residency documentation or awaiting the results of a required criminal-history background check.
Candidates listed as qualified have completed those reviews and have been determined eligible to appear on the ballot. The Department of Elections periodically updates the list as reviews are completed and additional filings are processed.
Minor parties also added candidates during August. The Independent Party of Delaware nominated Austin Cassidy for auditor of accounts, Carolyn Frank for the 5th Senate District and Steven Washington for the 1st Senate District.
The result is a November ballot with more contested races than Delaware voters appeared likely to see only a few weeks ago. Whether the late nominees can build competitive campaigns remains an open question. But in the districts where they qualified, voters will at least have a decision to make.
To-go box:

What happened: Delaware Republicans nominated 10 candidates after Aug. 1, including eight during the final week before the Sept. 1 deadline.
Why it matters: The nominations give more voters a choice between major-party candidates in November.
Historical context: It is the largest final-week group added by either major party in at least 16 years, based on Delaware’s available date-stamped records.
What’s next: Several nominees must complete state qualification reviews, while some November matchups will be determined by the Sept. 15 primary.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Vance attacks El-Sayed at Michigan GOP rally without mentioning trade war with Canada
description: U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Monday did not even once mention the nation’s ongoing trade war with Canada — and The White House’s politically charged renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America as a result — during a visit to Sterling Heights aimed at boosting President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidates in Michigan. Vance’s visit […]
text:
Vice President JD Vance speaking in Sterling Heights, Michigan on Aug. 31, 2026. (Courtesy of C-SPAN)U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Monday did not even once mention the nation’s ongoing trade war with Canada — and The White House’s politically charged renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America as a result — during a visit to Sterling Heights aimed at boosting President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidates in Michigan.
Vance’s visit was exclusively billed as a rally for Michigan GOP gubernatorial candidate U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township and U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers. Both spoke to supporters before Vance’s address. Trump made a similar visit to Michigan in July days before the August primary.
James will face Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson in the gubernatorial contest, and Rogers is up against Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. 
Vance asked Republicans to focus on the fight ahead, as the GOP views Michigan as a major battleground with control of the U.S. Senate, Congress, the Michigan Legislature and the state’s top executive offices all on the line in 2026. 
Vance put the various races’ stakes in stark terms: Choose candidates that have America’s back, or choose candidates focused on social and economic issues Americans rejected the last time Vance’s name was on the ballot.
“I’m sure that people who are paying attention to this race, they’re going to be able to point to this or that issue that they don’t agree with me on, or they don’t agree with the president, or they may not even agree with Mike Rogers on,” Vance said. “But that’s not the issue. Of course, you’re going to have disagreements with your elected officials because you’re free-thinking people who develop your own opinions. I’m not asking you to vote for Mike Rogers because you’re going to agree with him 100% of the time. I’m asking you to vote for Mike Rogers because he’s going to go to Washington and he’s going to fight for you.”


Vance labels El-Sayed as ‘evil’
Vance took aim at El-Sayed, hitting his campaign on multiple fronts. Vance at one point called El-Sayed “evil.”
“This guy is a goldmine of content, but unfortunately, it’s a goldmine of content of him fighting against the interests of the people in this room, and fighting for the most terrible ideas and terrible policies and the craziest ideas out there,” Vance said.
Vance mentioned El-Sayed’s comments in the aftermath of the Temple Israel attack in March, which El-Sayed apologized for over the weekend at a gathering of Jewish Democrats, but also his embrace of leftist streamer Hasan Piker, who has made controversial comments in the past about Israel, the state of American capitalism and about the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.
“I was trying to understand what would motivate a person to say these things … and I realized that there’s something about Abdul El Sayed that is very evil, and on the rise in the United States of America today,” Vance said. “It’s people who see themselves not as citizens of a common nation, fighting for every single person, whether they’re Jewish or Christian, whether they’re white or Black or brown, but see themselves as fighting for one group at the expense of others, and that is how, ladies and gentlemen, you destroy the United States of America.”
Vance asked that voters reject El-Sayed in November, and “reject the people that try to divide us one race against the other.”
Vance dodges talk of economic war with Canada
As Vance focused mostly on El-Sayed, he didn’t mention the ongoing trade tensions between the United States and Michigan’s neighbor to the north, Canada.
Trump recently announced new tariffs on Canadian-made goods, which are expected to further raise prices on goods sold in the United States. 
Trade talks have completely stalled between the U.S. and Canada, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Canadian Broadcasting Corporation News on Wednesday evening. The new tariff regime came a day after Canada announced retaliatory taxes to start Sept. 8 on $27.6 billion worth of American goods. 
Despite voters saying the high price of goods and services were a top concern, Trump moved forward to escalate his dispute with Canada.
James blames Michigan’s areas of decline on Benson
James said Vance’s appearance amid the trade war was a sign that a GOP win in Michigan was top of mind for the Trump administration. He said auto workers are still worried about the future of manufacturing, while parents in the Great Lakes state are worried about Michigan’s failing education system.
James said those were the products of Michigan under Democratic control, pointing to the party’s trifecta in which it controlled all three executive offices, the state Senate and the state House of Representatives for a two-year period in 2023 and 2024. The House has been under Republican control since 2025.
“Michigan families are paying too much for gasoline,” James said. “Our unemployment rate is above the national rate. Our children are falling behind. Infrastructure is struggling, and too many of our young people are leaving to find opportunity elsewhere.”
Some of those dynamics depend on decisions by federal policymakers and the president, while the state’s woes with educational attainment and literacy are issues both parties have struggled to address.
Still, that didn’t stop James from placing the blame on Benson and her gubernatorial running mate, state Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks.
“For nearly eight years, Jocelyn Benson in Michigan’s Democrat Party has been in leadership. For two of the years that President Biden was there, they had a full trifecta. They had the power. The Benson Brinks B team passed their agenda,” James said. “Our state is spending 50 percent more than it did under Governor Snyder. Do you feel like your child’s school is 50 percent better? How about your roads? How about your health care? No.”


Rogers calls El-Sayed a “con man.”
Rogers in his brief remarks called El-Sayed a “con man” for his positions on gender issues, criminal justice reform, abolishing ICE and his connections with Piker. El-Sayed is working to distance himself from Piker, and recently put out a statement saying that Piker does not speak for El-Sayed’s campaign.
Rogers said he was suspicious of El-Sayed’s attempts to do so now that he is a general election candidate.
“I was a former FBI agent. I busted swindlers and the mob, drug dealers, murderers, human traffickers, terrorists, and I have to tell you this: I know a con man when I see one,” Rogers said.
The Republican Party and its proxies have been accused of using Islamophobic tropes in their respective attacks on El-Sayed since he was elected as the nominee. They have also called the progressive candidate a communist and a socialist, even though El-Sayed has described himself as a capitalist who “understands how capitalism works.”
Rogers sought to distance himself from those lines of attack by saying his problem was not about how El-Sayed, who is Muslim and of Egyptian descent, prays or worships.
“This is not about your name,” Rogers said. “It is about the ideas that you have for big socialist government for our state and our country.”
Benson ties James to Trump’s tariffs
In a press conference held before Vance’s remarks, Benson excoriated Trump and Vance for manufacturing crises that she says have put the United States, and by proxy Michigan, in a precarious place at home and abroad.
Benson, along with former Democratic Michigan Gov. Jim Blanchard, who has endorsed Benson’s candidacy, noted that Trump’s tariffs have caused Michigan families to pay an extra $5,619 over the past year, the highest of any state in the nation, according to Axios.
Benson said James helped make that a reality by his unwavering support of Trump’s second term agenda.
“Because of his silence, he owns this. He owns these reckless tariffs. He owns this tax on Michigan,” Benson said. “So I’m going to call these tariffs what they are: they are a tax from John James, a John James tax on Michigan. The John James tax is a tax on our small businesses, on our gas prices, and a tax on our groceries.”
Benson added that, “as someone running to lead this state, I know the next governor has a moral responsibility to respond when someone hurts our state.”
“Michiganders deserve leaders who will never hesitate to stand up to anyone, no matter how wealthy or powerful, who threatens our residents or our state,” she said. “I’ve done that as Secretary of State, and I’m ready to do that as governor.”
Blanchard, who served as Michigan’s governor from 1983 to 1991, was also the U.S. Ambassador to Canada during the administration of President Bill Clinton. He called Trump’s tariff fight with Canada “totally destructive.”
“They’re going to cost us jobs and prices, car prices are already going up because of the tariffs on aluminum and steel and auto parts, as grocery prices are going up,” Blanchard said. “This is a major increase on the cost of living because of Donald Trump’s tariffs.”


El-Sayed calls Trump an ‘a**hole’ for picking on Canada 
Later in the afternoon, El-Sayed appeared in Warren with state Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak), who had competed against El-Sayed in the Democratic primary before dropping out in early July, along with several UAW workers to decry Rogers’ loyalty to Trump, working as Benson did to tie Rogers and Trump together.
“It shouldn’t be this hard to afford a second bag of groceries. It shouldn’t be this hard to pay your rent. It shouldn’t be this hard to see a doctor in the richest, most powerful country in the world,” El-Sayed said. “Meanwhile, Mike Rogers was fielding the call too. His call didn’t come from the people in the state of Michigan, it didn’t come from hardworking people across the state who understand that things need to get better and need to get better faster. It wasn’t about rooting out corporate corruption because he’s never seen a corporate check he did not want to take. It wasn’t about providing health care because he’s voted to raise your prescription drug prices 19 times.”
Instead, El-Sayed accused Rogers of running simply because Trump told him to do so.
“In fact, there’s nothing that Donald Trump will call him and tell him to do that he won’t willingly do. There is not a command he won’t ‘roger’ from the likes of Donald Trump or a corporation that’s willing to pay into his campaigns,” El-Sayed said. “Mike Rogers is corrupt, and he’s cowardly.”
El-Sayed also turned his attention to the trade war with Canada, saying that picking on a country that is often stereotyped for being the most polite was a choice.
“If you’re starting a trade war with Canada, it’s because you’re the a**hole. And here we are with Mike Rogers. He has no choice but to rubber stamp — to ‘roger’ — a trade war that is now costing the Michiganders that he says he wants to serve,” El-Sayed said. “This is a vanity war, and I want to be clear: this vanity war is not a war with Canada. It’s a war on Michigan because we have to pay the price.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Sheriffs drop license plate readers as DeSantis warns against ‘surveillance state’
description: Ron DeSantis insists no Florida governor has given law enforcement more tools to right crime than he has, but he wants them aimed at criminals, not citizens who have done nothing wrong. Speaking in Jacksonville Monday, the governor said he’s certain that nearly every sheriff in Florida can point to a situation in which Flock-style […]
text:
Flock camera (from Flock Safety's website)Ron DeSantis insists no Florida governor has given law enforcement more tools to right crime than he has, but he wants them aimed at criminals, not citizens who have done nothing wrong.
Speaking in Jacksonville Monday, the governor said he’s certain that nearly every sheriff in Florida can point to a situation in which Flock-style license plate-reading cameras have been used appropriately and “probably effectively.”
His concern, he continued, is how the data can be misused. His comments came three days after he said he wanted the state to remove those cameras from state right-of ways and after the Florida Department of Transportation said in a memo that it has revoked active permits for automated license plate readers.
On Monday at least four Florida sheriffs — Liberty County Sheriff Dusty Arnold, Clay County Sheriff Michelle Cook, Duval County Sheriff T.K. Waters and Putnam County Sheriff H.D. “Gator” DeLoach — said in separate statements that they have ordered discontinuation of the Flock system in their counties.
“After careful consideration, I have made the decision that the Liberty County Sheriff’s Office will begin the process of ending our contract with Flock Safety and discontinuing our use of the Flock camera system in Liberty County,” Arnold said in written statement posted Monday on social media.
“This decision comes in light of the continuing constitutional and privacy concerns surrounding license plate reader system, as well as Governor Ron DeSantis’ decision on Friday to remove Flock cameras from state right-of-ways.”
In Putnam County, Sheriff DeLoach has directed all 18 automated license plate readers in the county to be immediately disconnected and fully removed within 30 days.
“Over the past several weeks, legitimate questions have continue to emerge regarding privacy, data sharing, and government oversight and the future regulation of this technology,” DeLoach said, as reported by News4Jax. “I believe the responsible course is to discontinue our program and our contract at this time.”
Pasco County Sheriff Chris Nocco said Friday that his department would terminate Flock cameras by Sept. 30 following two consecutive county commission meetings in which commissioners voiced strong objections to the technology.
“Please know that the majority of the Board of County Commissioners’ lack of support for this agreement will impact the solvability of crimes and our ability to locate missing and endangered children and adults, including the victims of human trafficking. This will also cause a strain on the Sheriff’s Office [sic] already limited resources,” Nocco wrote.
Flock Safety has said that in a survey of nearly 700 law enforcement agencies, more than 40% “reported that our technology was involved in recovering half or more of the stolen vehicles in their jurisdiction.”
Still, Flock Safety in particular has come under torrents of criticism over its technology, which includes broad location data collection and sharing. There have been several publicized incidents demonstrating how local law enforcement officers have abused the technology, as such as the police officer accused in Polk County earlier this month of using Flock technology to track his estranged wife’s vehicle 717 times over a 21 months.
Data harvesting 
More than 200 cities and counties across the United States have terminated contracts with Flock Safety, according to data compiled by Social Justice, a California civil liberties advocacy group.
“I don’t want things that are sweeping up just everyday citizens and we’re told, ‘Oh yeah, don’t worry about it, no one’s going to use it.’ And then to find out some company, you know, is harvesting that and they can make a fortune,” DeSantis said.
“If they can make a dossier on your movement, they will be able to make a fortune in selling that to companies for advertising and for product placement and all of these other things.”
This issue has made it more relevant for the Legislature to come back to Tallahassee sometime before he leaves office in January to pass an ‘AI Bill of Rights,’ DeSantis said — legislation he tried to push through the Legislature this year.
The bill (SB 482) included a number of provisions related to interactions with chat bots but also would have banned AI companies from selling or disclosing personal information of users unless rendered as “deidentified data.”
The Florida Senate passed the AI Bill of Rights, 37-2, but the Florida House led by former Speaker Daniel Perez refused to bring the bill up for a vote, even after DeSantis called for the Legislature to do so in a special session focused on congressional redistricting this spring.
Perez resigned as Florida House Speaker earlier this month after he was confirmed by the U.S. Senate as U.S. ambassador to Brazil.
DeSantis noted that incoming Speaker Sam Garrison is likely to prove more amenable to the bill and said the Legislature could address it if the property tax amendment passes in November. Amendment 3 calls for an implementing bill to be passed by Jan. 1, 2027, if it if gets the 60% required from the voters, and suggested that could be the time for the Legislature to move on an AI bill.
“I’ve called for legislation that will protect Floridians from allowing the state to turn into some type of digital prison, digital surveillance state, where somebody knows everything about what you’re doing every day of the week,” he said. “You want to get in your car and you want to go to down to Buc-ees in St Augustine, it’s really none of the government’s damn business if you’re doing that, right?”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Buckle up! The energy bill roller coaster is about to begin.
description: The seasonal swings in energy bills will be a lot bumpier this year under a series of extra charges and discounts authorized by state utility regulators. The upshot: Rhode Island Energy customers will have to start paying more in fees beginning Sept. 1 under a $138 million revenue plan authorized by the Rhode Island Public […]
text:
Rhode Island Energy customers will see service fees increase Sept. 1, following a nine-month review by the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission.
(Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)The seasonal swings in energy bills will be a lot bumpier this year under a series of extra charges and discounts authorized by state utility regulators.
The upshot: Rhode Island Energy customers will have to start paying more in fees beginning Sept. 1 under a $138 million revenue plan authorized by the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission.  
Distribution rate increases were finalized under a series of unanimous votes by utility regulators on Aug. 21, though final bill impacts were not publicly available until Monday. 
The calculations mark the culmination of a nine-month review spanning thousands of pages of analysis and meetings among company consultants, state regulators and ratepayer advocates.
“It was quite an undertaking,” Commission Chairman Ron Gerwatowski said at a public meeting Monday. “It was a lot of schedules.”
Acknowledging the public interest in the long, complicated and confusing regulatory review process — namely, what it will mean for customers’ bills — Gerwatowski read aloud from a staff-prepared analysis on the expected bill impacts during the 15-minute meeting. 



Rhode Island Energy initially proposed a $230 million, two-year set of fee hikes, insisting that extra charges on the distribution side of the bill — separate from usage rates — were necessary to recoup the rising cost of  supplies, labor and new investments. The company also wanted to increase the maximum rate of return, or profit margin, from the existing 9.3% cap to 10.8%.
If approved as requested in November 2025, the company’s revenue generation plan would have raised average residential monthly electric bills by $7.78 and average annual gas bills by $343.53 in the first year. 
Ratepayer advocates, including the administrative arm of the state utility agency, the Division of Public Utilities and Carriers, argued against the new margin cap, which would have been higher than the 9.7% national average, and exceed caps for other utilities in New England. They also warned about the burden for Rhode Island ratepayers, who are struggling to keep up with existing bills amid the broader affordability crunch.
In the end, regulators kept the company profit margin cap as is, while cutting many of requested revenue increases related to company software expenses, legal fees and interconnection costs. And, they eliminated a second year of service charges in Rhode Island Energy’s proposal entirely.
As part of its decision, the commission also set up a framework for a $175 million discount plan required by the 2022 sale of the state utility operators to PPL Corp., Rhode Island Energy’s parent company. The credits are supposed to prevent customers from covering company tax costs associated with the transaction.
The company had originally pitched a lower, $149 million credit plan last year, but pulled back its offer amid accusations from Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha’s office that it was “lowballing” customers. The final, $175 million worth of credits is less than what Neronha’s office determined was owed, but more than the company proposed. 
“At the end of the day, this is about our customers,” Greg Cornett, Rhode Island Energy president, said in a statement on Aug. 25. “We believe delivering this additional relief is the right thing to do, particularly at a time when affordability remains a concern for so many Rhode Island families and businesses.”
Neronha accepted the end result of the negotiations.
“It just reaffirmed why it’s important that we push back on these issues,” Neronha said in an interview on Aug. 26. “If nobody pushes back, then the company will blow a fastball by Rhode Islanders.”
Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha accepted the end result of the negotiations with Rhode Island Energy, noting the importance of his office’s advocacy. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
The final calculations translate to a $14.51 monthly electric bill credit starting Oct. 1, and five months of gas bill credits, equal to $51.55, from Dec. 1 through April 30. The commission is expected to give final approval to the credit distribution at a scheduled meeting on Tuesday.
Separate seasonal electricity prices, set based on third-party suppliers, remain under consideration by the commission ahead of an Oct. 1 start date. 
Also awaiting a commission vote is a second set of bill credits drawn from the state’s gas cap-and-trade program, the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI). Gov. Dan McKee unveiled the proposed $28 million in RGGI discounts in July, which his administration says would save customers an average $20 per month on electricity bills during the first three months of the year. 
The commission is scheduled to consider both electricity usage rate hikes and RGGI bill credits in tandem at a Sept. 14 public hearing followed by an internal discussion meeting on Sept. 16.
McKee has repeatedly emphasized his focus on energy affordability in his reelection campaign, touting a controversial plan to save ratepayers more money by scaling back renewable energy and energy efficiency programs. The proposal was stricken from the final fiscal 2027 budget by lawmakers, prompting criticism from McKee.
“Energy affordability is my top priority,” McKee said in a statement on Aug. 21. “I will keep pressing this issue, and my administration will be back before the PUC to make the case again for putting ratepayer savings ahead of utility profits.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: How Danbury advocates are responding to major ICE operation
description: WSHU's Ebong Udoma and CT Mirror's Laura Tillman discussed a CT Mirror story about Danbury advocates' work amid significant ICE activity.
text:
More than 60 people were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) last week in Danbury. Advocates and officials are scrambling to keep up.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Laura Tillman to discuss her article, written with Katy Golvala and Sasha Allen, “In Danbury, some are hiding from ICE. Others are following them,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read their story here.
WSHU: Hello, Laura. You and your colleagues have done a fascinating behind-the-scenes look at how local activists deal with ICE activities in recent weeks. What prompted you to look into this?
LT: There was a press conference last Wednesday in Danbury where Senator Chris Murphy (D-CT) and Congresswoman Jahana Hayes (D-CT-5), Governor Ned Lamont (D), all spoke about a series of ICE arrests happening in Connecticut, and specifically focused on Danbury. The mayor of Danbury, Roberto Alves (D), also spoke at that press conference, as did some members of Danbury Unites for Immigrants, and it was clear that it was a very emotional press conference. It was kind of an unusual press conference to me as a reporter. I’d never seen, I don’t think, the governor, for example, leave the podium as he was answering a question because he was being shouted over by people in the crowd. The mayor of Danbury was also facing a lot of blowback from maybe between five to 10 people in the crowd who were kind of talking at times back to speakers or over speakers, sort of demanding answers or accountability.
So I just thought, wow, there’s a lot going on in Danbury right now. There’s a lot of emotion around this, and at the same time, it’s clear that there are people who have been doing a lot of work to support this to support this community, and sometimes when an elected official comes into town, you know there’s a way that that’s that can amplify an issue, but there’s also a way that maybe we don’t get to see all the grassroots work that’s been going on the other you know, 364 days of the year in this community. So I asked one of the members of the group if I could spend some time shadowing them and seeing this whole thing play out through their eyes and behind the scenes of what they’re experiencing.
WSHU: Now let’s talk about the woman from Hartford that you actually followed. She’s a volunteer with the Danbury Unites for Immigrants. That’s like a rapid-response team they’ve set up in Danbury. Now, could you talk about this woman and what drove her to take part in this, and what she actually experienced the day that you followed her?
LT: Yeah, I think that, you know, for a lot of people who are involved in this, they feel very intensely that they want to do everything they can to protect this community. The day that I spent with her and other members of the group, there was an event that happened in the morning where five people who were on their way to work, they were apparently being followed by ICE, and then there is video footage of what happened next, in which one of the men was pulled out of a car, lying face down, surrounded by agents, and then was tased multiple times by agents. Then those agents called 911 because the man was having trouble speaking. There was a discussion of him saying he had hypertension, so he was brought to the hospital. ICE agents were then at the hospital. The family and the attorney for the family were trying to gain access to the man in the hospital, and meanwhile, the rapid response team was just trying to do everything they could to support this family, to support this man, and see if they could get this man released.
WSHU: Now you spoke with the man’s nephew. What did he have to say? Just tell us a little bit about his nephew, and what did he have to say about this incident?
LT: So part of the story is also about kind of his experience of the day, trying to do what he could to help to go to the hospital to try to find medical records, to be in contact with attorneys, and kind of this this way that this family’s you know life is turned upside down by by this event with the tasing and and detainment of the uncle.
WSHU: Now let’s get back to Mayor Roberto Alves. Could you tell us a little bit about how he’s looking at this whole situation that’s happening as he leads the city of Danbury?
LT: Yeah, you know, the mayor is someone who has faced some criticism from members of the community that he hasn’t been doing enough to speak out. Mayor Alves himself does have this personal story in which he himself was an undocumented immigrant as a child and was brought here at age five from Brazil with his parents. So he does seem to have a lot of emotion and empathy about the experience of these children in his city and what they’re going through. I think at the same time he was expressing that there’s sort of more to it behind the scenes in terms of the push and pull of, you know, not wanting to turn his city into a target of this administration. He’s kind of in an interesting situation right now in terms of how he’s trying to negotiate with these different constituents and also just navigate this issue.
It kind of made me think of how Governor Ned Lamont has been kind of threading the needle at times with the Trump administration and speaking up about policies, but also trying not to make Connecticut sort of a specific target, the way that some other states have been targeted.
WSHU: In the meantime, it doesn’t seem as if ICE is going to change their tactics or slow down in any way.
LT: We didn’t hear about as much activity over the weekend, and you know, I think that we’ve seen these operations do kind of go from place to place. They come to a place, they target it for a while, and they move on. So it sort of remains to be seen in Connecticut how quickly that will happen. But we are watching to see, you know, what happens next with these kinds of arrests.
WSHU: Well, thank you so much, Laura. Really appreciate you doing this, and it’s a fascinating look at what is actually going on on the ground right now.
LT: Thank you.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Catron County residents seek local uranium mining ban after proposal clears first hurdle
description: Residents of the small west-central New Mexico town of Datil in Catron County gathered in an elementary school gymnasium last week to push local officials into action as a company makes steady progress toward exploring uranium deposits northwest of town.
text:
Residents of rural Catron County on Aug. 25, 2026, packed an elementary school gymnasium as they continue mounting opposition against a large uranium exploration effort north of Datil, N.M. (Photo courtesy Larry Basley) Residents of the small west-central New Mexico town of Datil in Catron County gathered in an elementary school gymnasium last week to push local officials into action as a company makes steady progress toward exploring uranium deposits northwest of town. 
NovaCore Exploration Inc. submitted a permit request July 2 to the state Mining and Minerals Division, seeking permission to drill up to 37 boreholes about 15 miles northwest of Datil for what it’s named the Ane Uranium Exploration Project.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The proposal, which comes amid a statewide spike in uranium interest, alarmed residents and New Mexico environmentalist groups, in part due to its size: If granted a permit to extract uranium, the company has claims covering 15,000 acres — roughly the size of the City of Carlsbad — which is far more than other recent uranium proposals across the state. 
Local activist Kathy Knapp told Source NM that approximately 70 people gathered in opposition in a town that U.S. Census records show contains 50 residents.
Two of the three Catron County commissioners, Buster Green and Audrey McQueen, spoke against the exploration effort at the meeting, though the commission has not taken any official action. McQueen and Commissioner Haydn Forward did not respond to Source NM’s requests for comment.
Green told Source NM on Friday that he, like nearly everyone else he’s spoken to in recent weeks, opposes the exploration project out of concern for the potential contamination of the underground aquifer. 
However, he said he is seeking more information from state officials before he pushes forward with a ban or other action. 
“We’re trying to get as much information as we can, so that we make good decisions, and also so that we can explain to the constituents of the county exactly what is going to be happening out there,” he said. 
The state Mining and Minerals Division Program Director DJ Ennis told Source NM on Monday that the state is beginning a technical review of the company’s proposed exploration effort after determining that its exploration permit is complete. That review includes determining whether the proposal meets criteria to be considered a “minimal impact” exploration project, a designation the company seeks. 
That designation means the project affects an area 10 acres or fewer and does not threaten water sources or use toxic chemicals like mercury or cyanide, among other state requirements.
If the MMD decides the exploration qualifies as a “minimal impact” project, no public hearing will be required.
Environmental advocacy groups, including New Mexico Wild, have asked the state agency to conduct a fuller environmental assessment and  a public hearing. 
“It’s the highest risk for contamination [in] exploratory mining you could ever do,” New Mexico Wild Gila grassroots organizer Luke Koenig told Source NM. “Not requiring a public comment period is just, I think, enraging the community.”
In response to Koenig’s concerns, Ennis stressed in the interview with Source NM that the state remains far from approving the exploration project and even farther from considering approval for an actual uranium mine. 
Catron County residents mobilize against ‘massive’ uranium mine proposal in Cibola National Forest

“It is not a proposed mine site,” Ennis said of the current proposal. “It is a proposed exploration.”
Ennis also noted the state has discretion to hold a hearing if it chooses and welcomes any public comment in the meantime.
NovaCore Chief Operations Officer Douglas Christopherson  did not return Source NM’s phone call Friday seeking comment. He previously told Source NM the company is committed to being a “good neighbor” while it determines whether, as a 1981 research paper concluded, up to 45 million pounds of uranium exist in the area.
Green told Source NM that additional public meetings will be held in the coming weeks to continue discussing the project. 
“We’re limited in Catron County,” he said of the county’s roughly 3,800 residents. “A lot of times, with federal and state government, it doesn’t seem like they’ve given us due diligence. They feel like they can come in and ride roughshod on us and do whatever they’re going to do.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Recount confirms 4-vote margin in WA Senate primary
description: Michael Shepard will be the Democratic candidate for a Bellingham-area Washington state Senate seat in November, after a recount confirmed his narrow primary victory over a fellow Democrat. Shepard, a Bellingham port commissioner, came into the hand recount up four votes on teacher Eamonn Collins after this month’s primary. The recount, certified Monday morn[...]
text:
Left, Eamonn Collins and, right, Michael Shepard. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)Michael Shepard will be the Democratic candidate for a Bellingham-area Washington state Senate seat in November, after a recount confirmed his narrow primary victory over a fellow Democrat.
Shepard, a Bellingham port commissioner, came into the hand recount up four votes on teacher Eamonn Collins after this month’s primary. The recount, certified Monday morning, didn’t change a single vote. 
Shepard defeated Collins by a vote of 13,125 to 13,121, in a primary with nearly 50,000 votes tallied. At one point during the initial counting, Collins clawed to within two votes of Shepard, but couldn’t surpass him. 
“We’re really pleased to be moving onto the general,” Shepard said Monday. 
Shepard added that the recount matching the initial machine tabulation “should provide everyone a huge amount of confidence in our election process here in Washington state,” especially given ongoing attacks on mail-in voting by President Donald Trump.
Whatcom County Auditor Stacy Henthorn agreed, calling the voting system “very accurate, very transparent.”
Collins didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment
Shepard and Collins were vying for a shot at an open seat in the 42nd Legislative District with Sen. Sharon Shewmake, D-Bellingham, forgoing reelection. Shepard will face Republican Erika Creydt, a psychologist and Blaine school board member, in November.
In Washington’s primaries, the top two finishers advance to the general election regardless of party affiliation. This year, election day is Nov. 3. 
As recently as 2022, a Republican senator represented the district, which covers north Bellingham and rural Whatcom County, including Ferndale, Lynden and Blaine, but it has tilted toward Democrats in recent years. 
Democrats feel good about their chances of retaining this Senate seat as the combined vote total for Shepard and Collins surpassed Creydt.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
On top of being a port commissioner, Shepard is an anthropology instructor at Western Washington University. He earned Shewmake’s endorsement. Collins, a science teacher at the Lummi Nation School, considered himself a grassroots progressive running to the left of Shepard’s more establishment lane.
Recounts rarely change election outcomes, but in a race this close, Collins was holding out hope for a shift. 
Statewide recounts across the country between 2000 and 2023 resulted in an average margin shift of 551 votes, representing 0.03% of the vote in those contests, according to an analysis by voting rights group FairVote. Recounts typically widen the gap between the top two candidates.

name: Daily Montanan
title: HUD secretary joins governor for foster youth housing discussion
description: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner praised strides Montana has made in reducing youth in its foster care system during a visit to the state last week. In a roundtable discussion hosted by Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte, Turner extolled Montana’s participation in First Lady Melania Trump’s Foster Youth to Independence program[...]
text:
Gov. Gianforte and HUD Secretary Turner hosting a roundtable discussion in Bozeman on Aug. 27, 2026. (Courtesy photo)
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner praised strides Montana has made in reducing youth in its foster care system during a visit to the state last week.
In a roundtable discussion hosted by Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte, Turner extolled Montana’s participation in First Lady Melania Trump’s Foster Youth to Independence program, which provides housing vouchers for young adults who are in or recently left the foster care system for up to three years. 
“Twenty thousand young people transition out of foster care every year … and one in four become homeless in a very short period of time — within four years — and that’s a serious challenge, and one that at HUD that we’re here to help to alleviate,” Turner said at a discussion in Bozeman. “At the same time, many are already working, continuing their education, making plans for their future. And our role at HUD is to help support that progress, to bridge the gap, and to create a pathway to greater independence for our foster youth.”
A closed-door roundtable discussion followed a few public comments, and included Montana State University President Brock Tessman, U.S. Rep. Troy Downing, former Montana foster youth, and nearly two dozen child welfare specialists and public housing authority representatives. 
Gianforte has made reducing the number of children in foster care a major priority for his administration, bolstering a refundable adoption tax credit for families who adopt from the state’s foster system and helping faith-based organizations recruit more foster families. 
In May, his office announced the number of children in the foster care system had nearly halved since he took office in 2021, and the state was joining a national collaboration to further strengthen the system. 
According to the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, there are 1,749 children in foster care around the state, down from more than 3,300 in early 2021.
Turner said during his remarks that reduction can be visualized as 30 school buses full of kids. 
“That is a tremendous feat, which I’m very proud. And it’s not an accident,” Turner said. “Montana has taken the steps to support adoption, strengthen partnerships with faith-based organizations, community organizations, and help young people in foster care build a strong foundation for the future. And that’s why I’m here.”
The Melania Trump Foster Youth to Independence program is an initiative first launched in 2019 during President Donald Trump’s first term, which awards housing vouchers to public housing authorities for adults under the age of 25 for up to 36 months. 
In Montana, just three of the state’s nine public housing authorities currently participate in the federal program, according to the governor’s office, with 40 vouchers administered in Butte, Billings and Missoula to date. More than 90% of those are actively housing youth. 
“One of the challenges with our programs were that the youth would have to become technically homeless to utilize this voucher,” said Sam Oliver, executive director of the Missoula Public Housing Authority. “We’ve really innovated in that department to connect with case managers and youth who are preparing to age out of care so we can create a more seamless transition.”
The roundtable discussion included two former foster youth, who shared their personal stories of using the vouchers to achieve self-sufficiency. 
Kyla Boggess, 24, recounted being in a domestic violence situation with the father of her child. 
“Without having the voucher, I would not be able to have moved out, and me and my child would have been stuck in that relationship,” Boggess said. “Now, since I’m not in that type of environment, I’m able to go to school, I’m able to have a meaningful job, and I’m able to not have to worry about things that would hinder that process.”
The federal initiative also provides funding and support for housing, education, employment and financial management through the John H. Chaffee Foster Care Program for Successful Transition to Adulthood. That program is administered through the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services Child and Family Services Division and helps bridge the gap for foster youth who age out of the program and are awaiting voucher approval for stable housing. 
Nationally, there are more than 8,900 Foster Youth to Independence awards currently effective through 409 public housing authorities in 49 states and the U.S. Virgin Islands, according to the governor’s office. 
“In the Bible, y’all, the Book of James says that we must ‘be doers of the word and not hearers only,’” Turner said in his remarks. “Tthat’s a good standard for us in public service to not only hear but then to execute. And at HUD, we’re listening and we’re acting, and we’ll continue to do so.”

name: VTDigger
title: More Vermonters are getting back their unclaimed property. Here’s how to find out if you have money waiting.
description:
Vermont is holding on to $175 million in unclaimed funds. Most can be accessed by a simple online form. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  More Vermonters are getting back their unclaimed property. Here’s how to find out if you have money waiting..
text:
Vermont State Treasurer Michael Pieciak speaks during a press conference marking Earth Day at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Wednesday, April 22, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
In his three years as state treasurer, one of Mike Pieciak’s proudest moments started with a list of names and allegations of a scam. 
He’d planned to attend the Putney Town Meeting two years ago, and part of his usual routine for visiting anywhere in Vermont was bringing along a printed copy of the state’s unclaimed property database for that community. But one line jumped out at him: A man with $38,000 waiting for him in the state account. 
Not wanting to wait on chance, he used some family connections to find the man and gave his daughter a call. 
“There was a period of time where they didn’t believe me,” Pieciak said. “Part of our challenge is that people have gotten really good at spotting scams,” since some common scams involve offering money over the phone. 
But he eventually convinced the man and his daughter of the truth. They realized it was a life insurance policy that the older man hadn’t known he was the beneficiary of, Pieciak said. 
The daughter sent Pieciak a thank-you note, saying, “ ‘We didn’t know about this money. We would never have looked for it,’ ” and getting the money meant her elderly dad could live in his house for another year, Pieciak said. 
Few Vermonters have that much money waiting in a state account for them to collect. But the Vermont Unclaimed Property Division is holding onto $175 million in funds that belong to Vermonters, according to treasury spokesperson David Kunin. And in many cases, all they need to do is fill out a form to claim it. 
Pieciak is running for his third term in the November general election against Republican Lynn LaFleur and Progressive Zachary Hample.
Pieciak sees the work of the division as a form of consumer protection. If a person or organization can’t be reached to get some money they’re owed — a last paycheck, a security deposit, a refunded bill — the payer can’t just take back the money. Instead, it must go to the state of Vermont in the hope its intended recipient will come collect it. 
“In the event a business closes, or the event that a business isn’t keeping its books very accurately, and that money disappears — that’s what we’re trying to avoid,” Pieciak said. “We’re trying to make sure that that money is protected, and then eventually it’s returned to Vermonters.”
Vermonters can see if they’re entitled to money on the Vermont-specific database on the treasurer’s website, or look across many states with missingmoney.com, the official website of the National Association of State Treasurers. 
In recent years, the number of Vermonters claiming their unclaimed property has been on the rise. It hit its peak in fiscal year 2025, when the treasury paid out to roughly 31,600 claimants.  
Pieciak said the division has done some outreach through TV and digital ads in the past two years that seems to be making a difference. “When you see that out and about, you see the claims going up,” he said. 
The division has also ramped up an automatic payment program called Money Back, where the state uses addresses from tax returns, “so we’re able to send them a letter that says, ‘we have $450 from the treasurer’s office, we will be sending a check to you in the next two weeks,’ and then we automatically send them the check,” Pieciak said. 
The program grew from 350 recipients in its pilot stage three years ago, to about 5,000 checks sent in the next year, then 1,000 the year after that, he said. 
The state receives unclaimed property every year around May 1, so Pieciak said he recommends that Vermonters check it regularly, although the funds are held by the state in perpetuity — there’s no time limit to when you can claim funds. 
The unclaimed property funds include both individual Vermonters and organizations, like businesses and nonprofits. When Pieciak hosts events with businesses and invites the local newspaper to come, it’s not unusual for him to tell them, “‘Hey, you also have unclaimed property,’” he said. As part of the reporting on this story it was discovered that VTDigger appeared on the unclaimed property list for an amount less than $100.
“Anyone that receives a lot of checks or writes a lot of checks — that’s almost every business — eventually, you’re going to have something that falls through the cracks,” he said.
